title: Planet Earth in One Level
objective: After this level you can name Earth's continents and oceans and say how much of the surface is water.
summary: About 71% of Earth's surface is water. The land splits into seven continents, and the water into five named oceans that are really one.

cards.headline: We named our planet Earth. Most of it is water.
cards.body: About 71% of the surface is ocean. Spin a globe, stop it with a finger, and you'll land on water about seven times out of ten. Maybe we should have called it Ocean.

cards.headline: Seven big pieces of land
cards.body: Everything that sticks up out of all that water is split into seven continents: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia. People live on all of them, with one exception. Antarctica has no permanent population at all; the only people there are researchers and the staff who support them. Nobody grows up in Antarctica.
cards.callout: Asia · Africa · North America · South America · Antarctica · Europe · Australia

cards.fact: Your old atlas may show four oceans. Most countries now count five.
cards.context: The classic four are the Atlantic, Pacific, Indian and Arctic. The fifth is the Southern Ocean, the water that encircles Antarctica. It's the newest named ocean, and National Geographic started recognizing it in 2021. So if you learned four, you weren't wrong. You were just early.

mascot.line: One ocean, five name tags. The water has never once read them.

cards.headline: Five names, one ocean
cards.body: Here's the twist: those five oceans aren't separate bodies of water. They all flow into each other. As NOAA, the US ocean agency, puts it, there is only one global ocean. The five names are like rooms in one big house. The walls are lines that people drew on maps, and the water ignores them completely.

title: Why Every Map Is Wrong
objective: After this level you can explain why every flat map distorts the round Earth and compare two common projections.
summary: A round Earth can't be flattened without distortion. Mercator's map keeps compass lines straight but inflates the far north and south; equal-area maps keep sizes true.

cards.headline: On many world maps, Greenland looks as big as Africa. Africa is 14 times bigger.
cards.body: Nobody drew it wrong on purpose. The mapmaker had an impossible job, and so does every mapmaker who ever lived.

cards.headline: The orange peel problem
cards.body: Peel an orange and try to press the peel flat on a table. It splits, stretches, or both. Maps have the same problem: Earth is round, paper is flat, and you can't get from one to the other without distorting something. A globe can keep size, shape, distance and direction all true at once. A flat map has to give some of them up.

cards.headline: Mercator's deal with sailors
cards.body: In 1569, Gerardus Mercator published a map built for navigation. On it, a straight line is a steady compass bearing: draw a line between two ports, hold that heading, and you're on course. The price was size. The farther a place is from the Equator, the more his map inflates it. Greenland sits far to the north, so it balloons.
cards.callout: Straight lines: great. Sizes: not so much.

cards.fact: Africa is about 14 times bigger than Greenland.
cards.context: On a Mercator map they look like rivals. An equal-area map fixes that: it shows every place at its true relative size, so Africa finally looks as huge as it is. The catch? Shapes come out stretched and squashed instead. No flat map wins at everything. Each one picks which truth to tell.

title: Latitude and Longitude
objective: After this level you can find any place on Earth using latitude and longitude.
summary: Latitude measures north or south of the Equator, longitude east or west of the Greenwich prime meridian. Together they pin down one spot.

cards.headline: Two numbers can find your front door. Or anywhere else on Earth.
cards.body: No street name, no city, no country. Just two numbers. Here's how the whole planet got a grid.

cards.headline: Latitude: how far north or south
cards.body: Picture rings around the globe, stacked like the rungs of a ladder from bottom to top. That's latitude. It measures how far north or south of the Equator you are: 0° at the Equator, up to 90° at the North or South Pole. The rings are parallel to each other, so they never meet. That's why they're called parallels.
cards.callout: 0° at the Equator, 90° at the poles

cards.headline: Longitude: how far east or west
cards.body: Now slice the globe like an orange, from pole to pole. Those lines are meridians, and they measure longitude: how far east or west you are, from 0° up to 180°. Unlike parallels, meridians all meet at the poles. But which slice is zero? Countries used to pick their own. In 1884 an international conference settled on one: the meridian through Greenwich, England.

mascot.line: Null Island: population zero, lost data plenty. I'd visit, but I'd need a boat and a very good excuse.

cards.fact: At 0°, 0° there's nothing but ocean.
cards.context: Where the Equator crosses the prime meridian, you're bobbing in the Atlantic Ocean, in the Gulf of Guinea off West Africa. Yet mapping software sometimes gives records with missing locations exactly those coordinates, so mapmakers jokingly call the spot Null Island. Give a place two good numbers, a latitude and a longitude, and it lands exactly where it belongs.

title: The Equator and the Tropics
objective: After this level you can explain what the Equator, the tropics and the polar circles mark and why they sit where they do.
summary: The Equator splits the hemispheres. Earth's 23.5° tilt sets the tropics, the only zone with an overhead Sun, and the polar circles, where days can last 24 hours.

cards.headline: Twice a year in Hawaii, flagpoles lose their shadows at noon.
cards.body: The Sun stands straight overhead, and the shadow hides right under the pole. Anywhere else in the US? Never. A few imaginary lines on the globe explain why.

cards.headline: The Equator: Earth's belt
cards.body: Start in the middle. The Equator is 0° latitude, exactly halfway between the North and South Poles, and it splits the planet into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Twice a year, at the equinoxes, the Sun passes directly over it. Every latitude you met in Level 3 is counted from this line.

cards.headline: The tropics: where the Sun turns around
cards.body: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so the spot where the noon Sun stands directly overhead drifts north and south through the year. It reaches the Tropic of Cancer, about 23.5° N, around June 21. Then it turns back and reaches the Tropic of Capricorn, about 23.5° S, around December 21. Between those lines lie the tropics, the only places where the Sun is ever directly overhead. Hawaii is inside. The rest of the US is not.
cards.callout: Overhead Sun zone: 23.5° N to 23.5° S

cards.headline: The polar circles: days that last all day
cards.body: Now go about 23.5° from each pole: that same tilt again. You reach the Arctic Circle at about 66.5° N and the Antarctic Circle at about 66.5° S. On these lines the Sun stays up for a full day at least once a year, and stays down for a full day, too. Keep going toward a pole and it stretches to six months. Try explaining bedtime there in June.

title: Time Zones
objective: After this level you can explain why the world has time zones and where the calendar date changes.
summary: Earth turns 15° an hour, so the world uses 24 time zones counted from Greenwich. The date changes at the International Date Line, near 180°.

cards.headline: Call a friend on the far side of the world and you might be calling tomorrow.
cards.body: It's Monday evening where you are, and your friend is eating breakfast on Tuesday. Nobody's clock is broken. The planet is round, and it spins.

cards.headline: Every town had its own noon
cards.body: Earth turns 360° in about 24 hours, which is 15° of longitude every hour. So the Sun reaches its highest point at a slightly different moment in every town. For centuries, communities set their clocks by their own Sun. That worked fine until railways spread, and a timetable had to juggle a different local time at every stop.

cards.headline: Twenty-four slices of time
cards.body: The fix was standard time. Cut the globe into 24 zones along meridians 15° apart, counted from Greenwich, and make each zone one hour apart. The system was adopted at the same 1884 conference that picked the prime meridian. On a real map, though, the borders zigzag, bending to follow countries' borders.
cards.callout: 15° of longitude = 1 hour

mascot.line: Head east over the line and you get yesterday back. I'd use mine to finish yesterday's crossword.

cards.headline: Where tomorrow begins
cards.body: Keep adding hours as you travel around the world and the days stop adding up. Something has to reset the calendar. That's the International Date Line, which roughly follows the 180° meridian, halfway around the world from the prime meridian. Cross it heading west and your calendar jumps a day ahead; head east and you get yesterday back. It even bends around the islands of Kiribati, so the whole country shares one date.

title: Compass and Directions
objective: After this level you can use the cardinal directions and explain how a compass finds north.
summary: North, east, south and west come from Earth's spin. A compass needle lines up with Earth's magnetic field, but magnetic north isn't true north.

cards.headline: Your compass doesn't point to the North Pole.
cards.body: It points somewhere nearby, and that somewhere keeps moving. The needle isn't broken. It's just loyal to a different north.

cards.headline: Directions for free, courtesy of the Sun
cards.body: North, east, south and west are the four cardinal directions, and east and west sit at right angles to north and south. The sky gives you a rough version for free: Earth spins toward the east, so the Sun rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west. Face the sunrise and north is on your left. Handy, but only roughly right, and no help at midnight.
cards.callout: N · E · S · W

cards.headline: A needle that feels the planet
cards.body: A compass needle is a tiny magnet, and Earth behaves like a giant one. Let the needle swing freely and it lines up with Earth's magnetic field. That's the big upgrade over the Sun: it works at noon or midnight, under clear skies or thick clouds. You're holding a sensor for the whole planet's magnetism in your palm.

cards.headline: Two norths
cards.body: Here's the catch. The Geographic North Pole sits at 90° N, the top of every meridian. The North Magnetic Pole is somewhere else, and it drifts over time. Your compass follows the magnetic one, so it's usually off from true north by an angle called magnetic declination. That angle changes depending on where you stand, so navigators look it up and correct for it.

title: Reading the Land
objective: After this level you can read elevation on a map and name landforms like plateaus, valleys and deltas.
summary: Heights are measured above sea level, and contour lines join points of equal height. Plateaus, valleys and deltas are three landforms to spot.

cards.headline: A flat sheet of paper can show you how steep a mountain is.
cards.body: No shading, no 3D glasses. Just a bunch of wiggly lines, if you know how to read them.

cards.headline: Every height starts at the sea
cards.body: Every height on a map needs a zero, and the usual zero is mean sea level. So when you hear that Mount Everest, the world's highest mountain, stands about 8,849 m tall, that means 8,849 m above the sea. Your hometown has a number like that, too. It's just less likely to be on a postcard.

cards.headline: Lines that never go up or down
cards.body: A topographic map draws contour lines, each one joining points at the same elevation. Walk along one and you'd never climb or descend. The trick is the spacing: lines bunched close together mean the ground rises fast, a steep slope. Lines spread far apart mean gentle ground. A cliff looks like a traffic jam of lines.

title: Continents and Oceans by Size
objective: After this level you can rank the seven continents and five oceans by size.
summary: Asia is the biggest continent and Australia the smallest. The Pacific is the biggest ocean, larger than all land combined; the Arctic is the smallest.

cards.headline: Every continent could fit inside the Pacific Ocean at once.
cards.body: All seven of them from Level 1, packed together, and the Pacific would still have room. Time to rank the whole planet.

cards.headline: The land league table
cards.body: Line the continents up by size and Asia wins easily, holding almost a third of the world's land. Next come Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica and Europe. Australia comes last: the smallest continent, and the flattest one, too. Last place, but it still gets to be a whole continent.
cards.callout: Asia › Africa › North America › South America › Antarctica › Europe › Australia

cards.fact: The Pacific covers about a third of Earth's surface.
cards.context: It's the largest and deepest ocean, and its area beats all the land on Earth combined. Then come the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern and, smallest of all, the Arctic. Remember, they're really one connected ocean. The Pacific just claims the biggest share.

cards.headline: Don't trust the wall map
cards.body: On a Mercator map, Antarctica looks gigantic. In the real ranking it's fifth, behind Asia, Africa and both Americas. Mercator inflates places the farther they are from the Equator, and Antarctica is about as far as you can get. When size is the question, trust the ranking, not the poster.

title: How Your Phone Knows Where You Are
objective: After this level you can explain how satellites let a phone pinpoint its location.
summary: GPS satellites broadcast their position and time. Your phone times the signals, turns them into distances, and uses four satellites to find itself.

cards.headline: Your phone never tells GPS satellites where it is. It just listens.
cards.body: The satellites only broadcast; your phone does all the math itself. That's also why the service is free for anyone, anywhere.

cards.headline: A sky full of clocks
cards.body: About 20,200 km up, at least 24 GPS satellites circle Earth, each one twice a day. They're spread out so that from almost anywhere, at least four are in view. Each carries a very precise atomic clock and keeps repeating the same message: here's where I am, and here's exactly what time it is.

cards.headline: Time becomes distance
cards.body: Your phone notes when each message arrives. The signal travels at the speed of light, so the delay tells your phone how far away that satellite is. Know how far you are from three satellites, and there's enough information to work out where you are. It's like counting the seconds between lightning and thunder to judge how far away a storm is, only with radio waves and far better clocks.

cards.fact: It takes four satellites, not three.
cards.context: The satellites' clocks are superb; the one in your phone isn't. At light speed, a tiny timing slip turns into a big miss. So your phone uses a fourth satellite to correct its own clock. The answer comes out as latitude, longitude and altitude: Level 3's two numbers, plus your height.

title: Checkpoint: Reading the Planet
objective: After this level you can use maps, coordinates, directions and time zones together to describe where any place is.
summary: A place's antipode is directly opposite through Earth's center: same latitude in the other hemisphere, 180° of longitude away, about 12 hours apart.

cards.headline: Dig straight down from the US. You won't reach China.
cards.body: Kids have been promised China for generations. Grab a shovel (a very long one), and let's check the claim with everything from Chapter 1.

cards.headline: The point exactly opposite
cards.body: Your antipode is the spot on the far side of Earth where a straight line through the center would pop out. Finding it takes Level 3's coordinates. Keep your latitude number but switch hemispheres, so north becomes south. Then go 180° of longitude around. Start from almost anywhere in the contiguous US and you surface in the Indian Ocean. Sorry, China.

cards.fact: Most of the world's land sits opposite ocean.
cards.context: Only about 15% of land has land on its far side. That's no shock after Level 1: about 71% of Earth's surface is water. Spain is one lucky exception. Most of New Zealand's North Island lies exactly opposite it.

cards.headline: Opposite in time, too
cards.body: Your antipode is 180° of longitude away, and Earth turns 15° an hour, so it's about 12 hours off from you. When it's noon where you stand, it's midnight there. Planning to call your antipode? One of you is going to be in pajamas.

title: Inside the Earth
objective: After this level you can describe Earth's crust, mantle and core.
summary: Earth has a thin rocky crust, a thick mantle of solid rock that slowly flows, and a metal core: liquid outside, solid inside. Earthquake waves revealed it.

cards.headline: The deepest hole ever drilled never made it through Earth's crust.
cards.body: Soviet scientists spent about 20 years drilling in Russia and reached 12,262 m. That's less than 0.2% of the way to Earth's center. So how do we know what's down there?

cards.headline: The crust: a thin shell
cards.body: You live on the crust, Earth's rocky outer layer. Under the oceans it's only about 5 to 10 km thick; under some continents it reaches 70 km. That sounds deep until you compare it with the trip to the center: about 6,371 km. Every beach, basement and mountaintop you'll ever visit sits in this thin skin. The planet's real bulk lies underneath.

mascot.line: Rock that flows but never melts. Geology loves a good contradiction.

cards.headline: The mantle: solid rock that flows
cards.body: Next comes the mantle, about 2,900 km thick and about 84% of Earth's volume. Forget the cartoon sea of lava. Grab a handful and it would be solid rock. Yet over long stretches of time it slowly flows, at about the rate your fingernails grow. Solid enough to hold, soft enough to creep.

cards.headline: The core: a ball of metal
cards.body: About 2,900 km down, rock gives way to metal: the core is almost entirely iron and nickel. The outer core is liquid, and its swirling creates Earth's magnetic field, the same field Level 6's compass needle lines up with. The inner core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun, yet it stays solid, squeezed by the immense pressure of the whole planet above it.

cards.fact: Nobody has ever seen the core. Earthquakes revealed it.
cards.context: Earthquakes send waves through the whole planet. One kind, S-waves, can't travel through liquid. Scientists noticed these waves vanish on the far side of Earth, as if something cast a shadow. That something was the liquid outer core, the only entirely liquid layer inside Earth. We found it by listening to the planet shake.

title: Plate Tectonics
objective: After this level you can explain how moving plates reshape continents over millions of years.
summary: Earth's outer shell is broken into plates that move a few centimeters a year. They pull apart, push together or slide past each other, and over millions of years that reshapes the map.

cards.headline: The Atlantic Ocean is wider than it was last year.
cards.body: Only by about 2.5 cm. But it's been at it for a very long time, and the reason is right under your feet.

cards.headline: A cracked shell
cards.body: Earth's outer shell isn't one piece. The lithosphere, the crust plus the top of the mantle, is broken into huge rocky plates, and they carry the continents and oceans with them. Remember Level 11's mantle, solid rock that slowly flows? The plates ride on that slowly flowing layer, pushed along by convection, heat circulating through the rock. Think of a cracked eggshell that won't sit still.

cards.headline: Slow, but it adds up
cards.body: Plates move about 2 to 15 cm a year. Useless for a day trip, unstoppable over time. Along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge they spread about 2.5 cm a year, and over 100 to 200 million years that turned a narrow inlet into the whole Atlantic Ocean. Patience, at planetary scale.

mascot.line: Plan a very, very long road trip. The destination is coming to you.

cards.fact: Los Angeles and San Francisco are creeping toward each other.
cards.context: They sit on opposite sides of the San Andreas Fault. The Pacific Plate slides northwest past the North American Plate at about 46 mm a year, roughly the rate your fingernails grow. Keep that up long enough and the two cities will be neighbors. No need to reschedule anything.

title: Pangaea
objective: After this level you can explain the evidence that today's continents were once joined.
summary: Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents were once joined in Pangaea. Matching coasts, rocks and Mesosaurus fossils backed him; plate tectonics finally explained how.

cards.headline: Africa and South America look like two halves of a torn page.
cards.body: Slide them together on a map and their coasts nearly click into place. It isn't a coincidence.

cards.headline: One land, one ocean
cards.body: In 1912, a German meteorologist named Alfred Wegener argued that the continents were once joined in one supercontinent. He called it Pangaea, from Greek for 'all the Earth', and a single global ocean, Panthalassa, surrounded it. About 200 million years ago Pangaea began to break apart, and its pieces became today's continents, the seven you met in Level 1.

cards.headline: The reptile that couldn't swim an ocean
cards.body: Coastlines were only the start. The rock layers of the two coasts match, too. Then there's Mesosaurus, a small freshwater reptile whose fossils turn up only in southern Africa and South America. It couldn't have swum the Atlantic. The simpler answer: it never had to, because the two continents were joined.

mascot.line: Right answer, missing homework. Science still checks your working.

cards.fact: Almost nobody believed him.
cards.context: Wegener couldn't explain what force could move whole continents, so most scientists rejected the idea. The answer came in the 1960s, when seafloor spreading and plate tectonics supplied the missing mechanism: Level 12's moving plates. Wegener had the what. He just didn't have the how.

title: Earthquakes
objective: After this level you can explain what causes earthquakes and how their size is measured.
summary: Stuck plate edges build up force until rock suddenly slips along a fault. Each step up the magnitude scale means about 32 times more energy.

cards.headline: Magnitude 6 sounds a bit worse than 5. It packs about 32 times the energy.
cards.body: Earthquake numbers climb in giant steps. But first: why would solid ground shake at all?

cards.headline: Stuck, then snap
cards.body: Remember Level 12's plates grinding past each other? Their edges are rough, so they get stuck while the rest of each plate keeps moving. Force builds and builds until it beats the friction. Then the rock suddenly slips along a fault, and that sudden slip is an earthquake. It's a heavy couch that won't budge, until it lurches all at once.

cards.headline: Where it starts, where you feel it
cards.body: The spot underground where the slip begins is the hypocenter. The point on the surface directly above it is the epicenter, the one that makes the news. From there, the energy spreads out as seismic waves, like ripples on a pond, and instruments called seismographs record them. They're the same kind of waves that revealed Level 11's liquid core.

cards.fact: Each step up the magnitude scale means about 32 times more energy.
cards.context: Each whole number also means ten times bigger swings on a seismogram. So a magnitude 7 releases about 1,000 times the energy of a 5 (32 x 32). The biggest ever recorded struck southern Chile on May 22, 1960: magnitude 9.5. Keep that one in mind; its story isn't over.

title: Volcanoes and the Ring of Fire
objective: After this level you can explain why volcanoes form where they do and locate the Ring of Fire.
summary: Magma rises because it's lighter than solid rock. Most volcanoes sit near plate boundaries, especially the Ring of Fire around the Pacific; Hawaii's sit over a hotspot instead.

cards.headline: Trace the rim of the Pacific and you've found most of the world's volcanoes.
cards.body: About 75% of them sit in one long loop. Where volcanoes grow isn't random. It's a map of the plates.

cards.headline: Why melted rock comes up
cards.body: Deep underground, some rock melts into magma. Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it rises. Where it breaks through the surface, you get a volcano, and the magma gets a new name: lava. The vast majority of eruptions happen near Level 12's plate boundaries.

cards.headline: The Ring of Fire
cards.body: Around much of the Pacific, plates meet and one dives beneath another. The sinking rock melts into magma that feeds volcanoes, strung along plate boundaries about 40,000 km long: the Ring of Fire. It holds about 75% of Earth's volcanoes, more than 450, and about 90% of its earthquakes. The Pacific, Level 8's biggest ocean, also has the busiest rim.
cards.callout: About 75% of volcanoes · about 90% of earthquakes

cards.fact: Hawaii's volcanoes are nowhere near a plate boundary.
cards.context: They sit mid-plate, more than 3,200 km from the nearest edge, over a hotspot: a stationary source of heat deep in the mantle. The Pacific Plate slides over it like paper over a candle. Each island gets carried off the hotspot in turn and its volcanoes die out. That's why the Big Island, still over it, is the youngest.

title: Tsunamis
objective: After this level you can explain how undersea earthquakes cause tsunamis and why they are so destructive.
summary: An undersea earthquake shoves the whole water column. The tsunami races across deep ocean as a low wave, then slows and piles up in shallow water; the sea may pull back first.

cards.headline: In 1960, an earthquake in Chile killed 61 people in Hawaii.
cards.body: Almost 15 hours after the shaking, something that had crossed the entire Pacific hit the town of Hilo. It wasn't the ground. It was the sea.

cards.headline: A shove from the seafloor
cards.body: A tsunami is a series of waves, usually set off by an undersea earthquake or eruption. When the seafloor suddenly lifts or drops, it pushes the entire column of water above it up or down, from the bottom to the surface. The name is Japanese for 'harbor wave'. The old name, 'tidal wave', is out: tides have little to do with it.

cards.headline: Fast and flat, then slow and tall
cards.body: Over deep ocean, a tsunami can travel as fast as a jet plane, yet it's at most a few meters high, spread over tens to hundreds of kilometers. Then it reaches shallow water near shore. It slows down, and all that moving water builds up higher and higher. The danger isn't out at sea. It's where the ocean runs out of room.

mascot.line: If the sea suddenly backs away, take the hint and back away too.

cards.fact: Sometimes the sea runs away first.
cards.context: Often the first part of a tsunami to reach shore is the trough, so the sea pulls back far from the beach. It looks like a curiosity. It's a natural warning sign: the rest of the wave is on its way.

title: How Mountains Rise
objective: After this level you can explain how colliding plates build mountain ranges like the Himalayas.
summary: India drifted north and collided with Eurasia 40 to 50 million years ago. Neither plate could sink, so the crust crumpled upward into the Himalayas, lifting old sea floor to Everest's summit.

cards.headline: There are fossil sea creatures at the top of Mount Everest.
cards.body: The highest rock on the planet, about 8,849 m above sea level, formed at the bottom of a sea. Something lifted it higher than anything else on Earth.

cards.headline: India on the move
cards.body: About 80 million years ago, India lay roughly 6,400 km south of Asia, riding its plate north at about 9 m a century. Then, 40 to 50 million years ago, it arrived. India collided with Eurasia, and the Himalayas began to form.

cards.headline: Nowhere to go but up
cards.body: In Level 15, one plate dove beneath another. Not this time. India and Eurasia have rock of about the same density, so neither could sink under the other. With the plates still pushing together, the crust had nowhere to go but up: it crumpled and thrust skyward. Shove two rugs together across a floor and watch them ruck up. Same idea, much bigger rugs.

mascot.line: Seashells at the summit. That's one very long commute from the seabed.

cards.fact: The Himalayas are still rising.
cards.context: India is still pushing into Asia, so the job isn't finished. That same push is how an old sea floor ended up on the roof of the world: the collision thrust fossil-packed limestone all the way to Everest's summit. Level 7 measured heights from sea level. Everest's top rock started out below it.

title: The Rock Cycle
objective: After this level you can name the three kinds of rock and explain how one turns into another.
summary: Igneous rock cools from molten rock, sedimentary rock is pressed from layers, and metamorphic rock is changed by heat and pressure. Any type can become any other.

cards.headline: A marble statue can start out as a pile of seashells.
cards.body: Rocks aren't forever. Given time, heat and pressure, one kind of rock turns into another. There are only three kinds to keep track of.

cards.headline: Igneous: cooled from molten rock
cards.body: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens. That's Level 15's magma underground, or lava once it erupts. Cool it slowly underground and it grows large crystals, like granite. Let lava cool fast at the surface and you get fine-grained rock, like basalt. Same melt, different patience.

cards.headline: Sedimentary: built in layers
cards.body: Weathering breaks rock into pieces and erosion carries them off. Those bits, plus the remains of living things, settle in layers, and the lowest get pressed into solid rock: sedimentary rock. Limestone is often built from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures. That's what Level 17's Everest summit is made of.

cards.headline: Metamorphic: changed, not melted
cards.body: Metamorphic rock is any rock changed by heat and pressure without melting. Bake and squeeze limestone and you get marble; do it to granite and you get gneiss. And it keeps going: any type of rock can become any other. The rock under your feet is just between jobs.

title: Wind, Water and Ice
objective: After this level you can explain how erosion carves canyons, valleys and coastlines.
summary: Weathering breaks rock down; erosion carries it away. Water carved the Grand Canyon, glaciers grind U-shaped valleys, waves cut arches and stacks, and wind shapes dunes.

cards.headline: The Grand Canyon was dug by a river.
cards.body: No colliding plates, no volcano. The Colorado River started carving about 5 to 6 million years ago, and the canyon is now about 1.6 km deep.

cards.headline: Break it, then move it
cards.body: Two jobs shape the land. Weathering breaks down or dissolves rock where it sits. Erosion wears material away and carries it off, and liquid water is the biggest carrier on Earth. The Colorado River had help: in floods it hauls large rocks that act like chisels, chipping pieces off its own bed. Wind and glacial ice erode, too.

cards.headline: V for river, U for ice
cards.body: Remember Level 7's valleys? Rivers cut them into a V. Glaciers grind them into a wide U. And the eroded bits have to land somewhere: where a river slows at its mouth, it drops its sediment and builds a delta. Erosion doesn't destroy land so much as move it.

mascot.line: Water, wind and ice: the slowest demolition crew on Earth, and the most thorough.

cards.headline: Coasts and deserts
cards.body: At the coast, waves bore caves into cliffs. When a cave breaks through, it becomes an arch; keep the waves coming and you're left with rock columns called sea stacks. In deserts, wind does the carving, sculpting rock and piling sand into dunes. Same job, different tools.

title: The Water Cycle
objective: After this level you can describe how water moves between the ocean, the sky and the land.
summary: The Sun lifts water into the sky and gravity brings it back down. Most vapor rises from the sea, spends about 10 days aloft, and the total never changes.

cards.headline: The rain on your window has made this trip before.
cards.body: Earth doesn't make fresh batches of water. It keeps moving the same supply around, from sea to sky to land and back again. That loop is the water cycle, and every glass you drink is borrowed from it.

cards.headline: The Sun lifts, gravity drops
cards.body: The whole loop runs on two engines. Energy from the Sun warms water until it evaporates and rises as invisible vapor. Up high, the vapor condenses into clouds. Then gravity takes over: the water falls as rain or snow and makes its way back across and under the land. The Sun does the heavy lifting. Gravity handles the delivery, free of charge.

cards.fact: About 90% of the water vapor in the air rose from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers.
cards.context: That's no surprise after Level 1: about 71% of Earth's surface is water, so most evaporation starts at sea. Most of the rest comes from plants, which release vapor through tiny pores in their leaves. That's called transpiration. A tree on a hot afternoon is quietly sweating into the sky.

mascot.line: Ten days in the sky, then back to work. Water has a stricter schedule than I do.

cards.headline: A short stay in the sky
cards.body: Once a water molecule evaporates, it spends about 10 days in the air on average, then falls back down. So the sky isn't a storage tank; it's a waiting room. And through all this moving, the total amount of water in the cycle stays essentially constant. Nothing new arrives and nothing is used up. The water just keeps changing places.

title: One World Ocean
objective: After this level you can name the five oceans and explain why they are really one connected ocean.
summary: Seas are smaller corners of the ocean, usually partly enclosed by land, and the five named oceans are regions of one ocean. At its deepest, it could swallow Everest.

cards.headline: There is a sea with no shore anywhere.
cards.body: Picture a sea and you probably see a beach around the edge. The Sargasso Sea, out in the Atlantic, has no coastline at all. Ocean currents alone draw its edges. So what makes a sea a sea, and where does one ocean end?

cards.headline: Seas are corners of the ocean
cards.body: A sea is smaller than an ocean. It usually lies where land and ocean meet, and it's typically partly enclosed by land. If the ocean is a big house, seas are its alcoves. The Sargasso is the odd one out: the only sea with no land boundary at all. It's a room whose walls are made of moving water.

cards.headline: Five names, still one ocean
cards.body: Remember Level 1's oceans? From largest to smallest: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. They're not five tanks. They're connected regions of one global ocean, divided by lines people drew. That's how a sea can float in the middle of the Atlantic with no shore. The borders were only ever on paper.

cards.fact: The ocean's deepest known point is about 11 km down.
cards.context: It's called Challenger Deep, in the Pacific's Mariana Trench. Level 7's Mount Everest stands about 8,849 m tall. Set it on the bottom of Challenger Deep and its peak would still be about 2 km underwater. Most of the ocean is shallower, with an average depth of about 3,700 m. That's still a long way to swim.

title: Ocean Currents
objective: After this level you can explain how currents like the Gulf Stream carry heat around the planet.
summary: Winds drive surface currents that carry warm water toward the poles; the Gulf Stream helps keep Norway mild. Deep down, dense water drives a loop that takes about 1,000 years.

cards.headline: In 1992, thousands of bath toys went to sea by accident.
cards.body: A container ship in the North Pacific lost a box holding about 29,000 plastic bath toys. Nobody planned it, but you couldn't design a better experiment: a flotilla of floating markers, all launched from one spot.

cards.headline: Pushed by the wind
cards.body: About ten months later, the first toys washed up in Alaska. Some eventually drifted all the way into the Atlantic. What carried them? Surface currents, and their engine is the wind: winds drive the currents at and near the ocean's surface. Every duck on a beach was a pin in the map showing where the water had gone.

mascot.line: Norway gets its winter heating piped in from Florida. The plumbing is just very, very long.

cards.headline: The ocean's central heating
cards.body: Currents don't just move bath toys; they move heat. They carry warm water from the Equator toward the poles and bring cold water back. The Gulf Stream is the famous one: a warm current that flows north along Florida, then turns northeast across the Atlantic, forming the western edge of Level 22's Sargasso Sea. It helps give Bergen, Norway, milder winters than New York, much farther south.

cards.fact: One lap of the deep ocean's 'conveyor belt' can take about 1,000 years.
cards.context: Deep down, the wind can't reach, so density does the pushing. Cold, salty water is dense and sinks, while warm water stays near the surface. That sinking keeps a slow loop turning through the deep ocean. Next to the Gulf Stream, it's a sloth on a treadmill.

title: Coasts and Beaches
objective: After this level you can explain how waves build and wear away coastlines.
summary: Wind makes waves that carry energy to the coast. They carve arches that collapse into sea stacks, and longshore drift moves beach sand along the shore.

cards.headline: In 2005, a 50 m tower of rock off Australia fell into the sea.
cards.body: It was one of the Twelve Apostles, limestone pillars standing in the surf off Victoria. What knocks down a tower of rock? The same thing that builds a beach.

cards.headline: Wind makes the waves
cards.body: Most ocean waves start with wind, from friction between moving air and the water's surface. Waves carry energy, not water, and they can travel across an entire ocean before they hit anything. Then all that energy slams into the coast. The wind blows on one side of an ocean, and a cliff takes the punch on the other.

cards.headline: Arch today, stack tomorrow
cards.body: Aim waves at rocky cliffs for long enough and they can carve a sea arch right through the rock. When the arch collapses, one leg is left standing alone in the water: a sea stack. That's what the Twelve Apostles are. And the waves don't stop. Further erosion wears a stack down until it disappears, which is how Australia lost an Apostle in 2005.

cards.headline: The beach is on the move
cards.body: Waves don't only take; they carry. They usually reach a beach at a slight angle, which sets up a longshore current running parallel to the shore. Beach sand rides along with it. That's longshore drift, and it can strip a beach badly. The beach you visit every summer isn't quite the same beach. Its sand has been quietly heading down the coast.

title: Lakes and Inland Seas
objective: After this level you can explain how lakes form and why some, like the Dead Sea, are salty.
summary: Lakes fill basins dug by glaciers or by the crust pulling apart. A lake with no outlet loses water only by evaporation, so its salt builds up, as in the Dead Sea.

cards.headline: The Dead Sea is a lake. So why is it saltier than the sea?
cards.body: It's nearly ten times saltier than the ocean, and you can lie back and float like a pool toy. To see why, start with how any lake gets made.

cards.headline: First, dig a bowl
cards.body: A lake is a large body of standing or slowly moving water that fills a basin inland, so something has to dig the basin. Glaciers have made more lake basins than anything else, especially in the Northern Hemisphere; a retreating ice sheet shaped North America's Great Lakes. Earth's crust digs some too. Siberia's Lake Baikal fills a rift where the crust is breaking apart. It's the deepest and oldest lake on Earth, and it holds about a fifth of the fresh water on the planet's surface.

cards.headline: Where the salt comes from
cards.body: Rain slowly dissolves minerals from rocks, and rivers carry them downstream. That's where the ocean's salt comes from. Now picture a lake with no outlet. It can lose water only by evaporation, and evaporation takes the water but leaves the salt. Year after year, the salt stays and the lake grows saltier. It's a bathtub that fills from the tap and never drains.

cards.fact: The Dead Sea is nearly ten times saltier than the ocean.
cards.context: The Jordan River supplies nearly all its water, and nothing flows out. Water leaves only by evaporation, so the salt piles up. The water is so dense that bathers float easily, and apart from bacteria, nothing lives in it. Not so dead after all, if you're a microbe.

title: Glaciers and Ice Sheets
objective: After this level you can explain how glaciers form and how much fresh water they hold.
summary: Glaciers form where snow survives year after year and is squeezed into ice that flows downhill. Earth's two ice sheets hold over 68% of its fresh water.

cards.headline: A glacier is snow that refused to melt.
cards.body: No freezer required. Just snow that lasted through summer, then got buried by next winter's snow, again and again, until it became a river of ice.

cards.headline: From snowflake to ice
cards.body: A glacier starts where snow lasts all year and piles up. Each new layer buries and squeezes the ones below. The buried snow recrystallizes into grains about the size and shape of sugar, then packs tighter until it's solid ice. And ice that heavy doesn't sit still: it slowly flows downhill under its own weight. A mountain glacier is a frozen river in extreme slow motion.

cards.headline: Rivers of ice leave a U
cards.body: Remember Level 7's valleys? Rivers cut a V; glaciers grind a U. That's the flow at work: a glacier doesn't just sit on a mountain, it slowly moves down it and reshapes the valley as it goes. When the ice finally melts away, the U stays behind as proof it was there.

mascot.line: Most of the planet's fresh water is sitting in two giant freezers. Please don't unplug them.

cards.headline: Two giants
cards.body: Ice sheets are glaciers on a continental scale, and Earth has just two today: one covers most of Greenland, the other spans Antarctica. Together they hold over 68% of all the fresh water on Earth. If the whole Antarctic Ice Sheet melted, sea level would rise about 58 m. That's a lot of water parked on land.

title: Fresh Water Is Rare
objective: After this level you can explain how little of Earth's water is fresh and easy to reach.
summary: Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh. Most of that is frozen or underground in aquifers, and just a sliver sits in lakes and rivers.

cards.headline: A planet made of water, and you can barely drink any of it.
cards.body: Level 1 told you water covers about 71% of Earth's surface. So how can fresh water ever be scarce? Because only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh.

cards.headline: The 100-liter tub
cards.body: Imagine all of Earth's water poured into a 100-liter tub. About 96.5 liters is ocean, and it's salty. Only about 2.5 liters is fresh. Now take out the ice caps, the glaciers and the groundwater. What's left at the surface, including every lake and river on Earth, is about 30 mL. That's two tablespoons in a full tub.

cards.headline: Frozen or buried
cards.body: Where's the rest of the fresh water? Over 68% of it is locked in ice and glaciers, much of it in Level 27's two ice sheets. About 30% is underground. Only a little over 1.2% sits at the surface. Yet rivers are the source of most of the fresh surface water people use. We live on the leftovers of the leftovers.

cards.headline: Not an underground river
cards.body: The underground share isn't flowing through secret rivers. Groundwater fills tiny pores and cracks in soil and rock, moving more like water in a sponge. It's found in usable amounts only in certain places, called aquifers, and people reach it by digging wells. Next time you see a well, picture a straw stuck into a giant wet sponge.

title: River Valleys and the First Farms
objective: After this level you can explain why river valleys and deltas drew the first farms and cities.
summary: River valleys gave early farmers water and fertile soil. The Nile's yearly flood left silt so dark that Egypt was named Kemet, 'black land'.

cards.headline: Ancient Egypt named itself after mud.
cards.body: Egyptians called their land Kemet, 'black land'. Not for the pyramids or the desert: for the dark, fertile silt the Nile's flood left behind every year.

cards.headline: A river that fertilized its own fields
cards.body: Every summer the Nile flooded its valley, then drained away and left fresh silt, the sediment the river had carried. That silt worked as a natural fertilizer, so farmers could grow crops to feed a dense population. The flood came every year until the Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970. Until then, Egypt's farms got a delivery they never had to order.

cards.headline: Between the rivers
cards.body: Egypt wasn't alone. Many of the earliest civilizations grew up in river valleys good for farming: Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus valley and China's Yellow River valley. Mesopotamia wears it in its name, from a Greek word meaning 'between rivers', the Tigris and the Euphrates. Its farmers dug branching canals to carry river water to large stretches of dry land.

cards.fact: The Fertile Crescent, often called the 'cradle of civilization', is named for its rich soils.
cards.context: It lies in the Middle East, watered by the Tigris and Euphrates, with the Nile running through part of it. Farming and irrigation took hold there because of the fertile soil near those rivers. Civilization, it turns out, started out with muddy boots.

title: Checkpoint: Water World
objective: After this level you can trace water through the oceans, rivers, ice and the water cycle.
summary: In the last ice age so much water was frozen on land that the sea fell about 120 m and Beringia linked Asia to Alaska. Ice and ocean trade the same water.

cards.headline: You could once walk from Asia to Alaska. No boat needed.
cards.body: Where the Bering Strait's seafloor lies today, there used to be dry land linking Siberia with Alaska. So where did the sea go? Everything from this chapter points to the answer.

cards.headline: The water was parked on land
cards.body: Remember Level 21: the total amount of water in the cycle stays essentially constant. It only changes places. During the last ice age, so much water was frozen in glaciers that sea level fell by as much as about 120 m. Ice sheets covered the northern third of North America and much of northern Europe. The ocean hadn't lost that water. It was on land, as ice.

cards.headline: A bridge made of seafloor
cards.body: With the sea that low, the floor of today's Bering Strait became dry land, called Beringia. Plants and animals moved across it, and people followed that route in search of game. The bridge is still there. It's just under the water again.

cards.headline: The loop runs both ways
cards.body: Now run the tape forward. Level 27's ice sheets still hold over 68% of Earth's fresh water. If the whole Antarctic Ice Sheet melted, sea level would rise about 58 m. Ice and ocean share one account: freeze more water and the sea drops; melt it and the sea rises.

title: Weather or Climate?
objective: After this level you can tell weather from climate and explain why the difference matters.
summary: Weather is the atmosphere's short-term mood; climate is a place's average weather over decades, usually 30-year averages. One cold day is weather, not climate.

cards.headline: You check the weather to get dressed. You check the climate to pack.
cards.body: Same sky, two very different questions. Mix them up and you'll bring a parka to a beach holiday.

cards.headline: Weather: right now
cards.body: Weather is what the atmosphere is doing at the moment: sunny, rainy, windy, freezing. It can change from minute to minute, hour to hour and day to day. That's why you check it every morning, and why the forecast for your picnic can flip by lunchtime. Weather is the sky's mood.

cards.headline: Climate: what's normal
cards.body: Climate is the average weather of a place over a long stretch of time. Those averages usually cover 30 years. NOAA's current US averages, called climate normals, cover 1991 to 2020, and they're refreshed every 10 years. Think of weather as one page of a diary. Climate is the whole diary, summed up.
cards.callout: Climate is what you expect. Weather is what you get.

mascot.line: My umbrella answers to the weather. My closet answers to the climate. My socks refuse to take sides.

cards.headline: Why the difference matters
cards.body: Weather tells you what to wear each day. Climate tells you what clothes to keep in your closet. The difference also stops you from reading too much into one day. Even as the planet warms, blizzards and freezing days still happen; over time they just happen less often. One cold morning is weather. A trend across decades is climate.

title: Why the Equator Is Hot
objective: After this level you can explain how the angle of sunlight makes the tropics warm and the poles cold.
summary: Near the Equator sunlight lands almost straight down on a small area; toward the poles it slants and spreads out. Tilt, not distance, makes the seasons.

cards.headline: The word climate comes from the Greek for 'slope.'
cards.body: Not a hillside. The slope of the Sun's rays. Whoever named it was onto something: how warm a place gets is mostly about the angle.

cards.headline: Same sunlight, different angle
cards.body: Near the Equator, the midday Sun shines almost straight down, so its energy lands on a small patch of ground. Toward the poles, the same sunlight arrives at a low slant and spreads over a much bigger area. Try it with a flashlight: point it straight at a table and you get a small, bright circle. Tilt it and the light smears into a wide, dim oval. Same flashlight, less heat per spot.

mascot.line: Closest to the Sun, and people are scraping ice off their windshields. Angles beat distance every time.

cards.fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
cards.context: That's the middle of winter in the Northern Hemisphere, so distance can't be what makes summer hot. Earth's tilt is. In June the Northern Hemisphere's sunlight hits most directly, and it gets summer. Remember Level 4's tropics? They're the only places where the Sun ever shines straight overhead.

cards.headline: The planet's heat delivery service
cards.body: Add it up and the tropics collect the most solar energy, while the Arctic and Antarctic get the least. That imbalance never settles, because the atmosphere and oceans keep carrying the extra heat toward the poles, through winds, currents and weather. The rest of this chapter is the story of that delivery service.

title: Wind and Pressure
objective: After this level you can explain how differences in air pressure make wind, including the trade winds.
summary: Wind is air flowing from high to low pressure. Uneven heating makes the highs and lows; Earth's spin bends the flow into the easterly trade winds.

cards.headline: For centuries, sailing ships crossed the Atlantic on winds they could count on.
cards.body: They carried ships from Europe and Africa to the Americas, and sailors called them the trade winds. To see where they come from, start with a simpler question: why does air move at all?

cards.headline: Air hates a crowd
cards.body: Air presses on everything, and in some places it presses harder than in others. Air flows from high pressure toward low pressure, the way passengers on a crowded bus spread into the empty seats. That flow is wind. The bigger the pressure difference, the faster the wind blows. A gentle breeze means a small difference. A gale means a big one.
cards.callout: Wind blows from high pressure to low pressure.

cards.headline: The Sun sets the pressure
cards.body: So where do the highs and lows come from? From Level 32's uneven sunshine. Warm air rises, leaving low pressure below it. Cool air sinks and makes high pressure. Near the Equator, strong heating lifts warm, moist air like a hot-air balloon, and air from both sides flows in to replace it. The heat delivery service has an engine, and it runs on pressure.

mascot.line: The air aims straight, and the planet turns the corner for it. Very polite of Earth, really.

cards.headline: Trade winds, with a twist
cards.body: That inflowing air never blows straight at the Equator, because Earth spins underneath it. The spin deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern. That's the Coriolis effect. It bends the flow into the trade winds: steady easterlies near the Equator, blowing from the east toward the west. Handy, if your ship is heading for the Americas.

title: Rain Shadows
objective: After this level you can explain why one side of a mountain range can be wet and the other dry.
summary: Mountains force moist air up, where it cools and rains on the windward side. The air sinks, warms and dries on the leeward side: a rain shadow.

cards.headline: Hawaii's famous sunny beaches are on the dry side of the islands.
cards.body: Waikiki on Oahu and Wailea on Maui sit on the sheltered sides of their islands, where it's sunnier and drier. The other sides are lush and green. The mountains in between decide who gets the rain.

cards.headline: Up the mountain: rain
cards.body: Wind pushes moist air toward a mountain range. The air has nowhere to go but up, and as it rises it expands and cools. Cool air holds less moisture than warm air, so the water vapor condenses into clouds and falls as rain or snow. The slope facing the wind, the windward side, gets soaked. The mountain has basically wrung the air out like a sponge.

cards.headline: Down the other side: the shadow
cards.body: Once the air crosses the peaks and sinks down the far side, the leeward side, it warms up and its clouds clear. There's little rain left to give. That dry zone behind the mountains is a rain shadow. Death Valley sits in one, and it's the driest place in North America, averaging less than 5 cm of rain a year.
cards.callout: Windward: wet. Leeward: dry.

cards.headline: Back to Hawaii
cards.body: Now the beaches make sense. Level 33's trade winds pick up moisture as they blow across the ocean. When they hit an island's mountains, the air rises and drops its rain on the windward side, which stays lush and green. The leeward side sits in the rain shadow, sunnier and drier. The beach towels go where the rain doesn't.

title: Monsoons
objective: After this level you can explain how seasonal winds bring monsoon rains to South Asia.
summary: A monsoon is a seasonal wind reversal. In summer, hot land draws moist ocean air over South Asia, bringing most of India's rain; in winter the wind turns and dries.

cards.headline: A monsoon isn't a rainstorm. It's a wind that changes its mind.
cards.body: A monsoon is a seasonal change in the direction of a region's main winds. The word comes from the Arabic mawsim, meaning season. And the season it brings can make or break a year's harvest.

cards.headline: Land heats faster than water
cards.body: Picture a beach in summer: the sand burns your feet while the sea stays cool. Land heats up faster than water, and a whole continent does the same. In summer, low pressure forms over the hot land. You know Level 33's rule: air flows from high pressure to low. So moist air from the cooler ocean pours inland.

cards.headline: South Asia's summer soaking
cards.body: In South Asia, the summer monsoon blows in off the Indian Ocean from the southwest, from about June to September, bringing heavy rain. About three-quarters of India's yearly rain falls in those months. Farther north, the Himalaya squeeze the air dry, leaving the Tibetan Plateau in a rain shadow. In winter the pattern reverses: winds blow from the northeast and the weather turns mostly dry.
cards.callout: Summer: from the southwest, wet. Winter: from the northeast, dry.

mascot.line: Imagine your whole year depending on which way the wind decides to blow. Suddenly my weather app feels trivial.

cards.headline: Too little, too much
cards.body: Farms across South Asia depend on the monsoon. When the rains come late or weak, harvests suffer. When they come too hard, floods follow. Same wind, very different years, and a huge part of the world watches the sky to see which one it's getting.

title: Hurricanes and Typhoons
objective: After this level you can explain how tropical storms form and why they have different names in different oceans.
summary: Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are one kind of storm, named by ocean. They feed on warm water, spin with the Coriolis effect and weaken over land.

cards.headline: A hurricane, a typhoon and a cyclone walk into a bar. They are the same storm.
cards.body: They're all tropical cyclones. The only difference between them is where on the ocean the storm happens.

cards.headline: Built on warm water
cards.body: A tropical cyclone starts over ocean water of about 27°C (80°F) or warmer. The water evaporates, and warm, moist air rises, cools and condenses into towering clouds. Once its sustained winds reach 119 km/h (74 mph), it's officially a hurricane or typhoon. Push it over land and it's cut off from its warm, moist ocean air, so its winds weaken. No warm water, no fuel.

cards.headline: The spin comes from Earth
cards.body: Here's Level 33's Coriolis effect again. It makes these storms spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern. But the Coriolis effect is zero at the Equator, so a storm there has nothing to get it spinning. That's why tropical cyclones form some distance away from the Equator, even though the water there is plenty warm.

title: Thunderstorms and Tornadoes
objective: After this level you can explain how thunderstorms, lightning and tornadoes form.
summary: Thunderstorms need moisture, unstable air and lift. Lightning heats air so fast it booms as thunder; tornadoes are rotating columns of air from a storm to the ground.

cards.headline: See lightning, then count. About 3 seconds of silence means about 1 km away.
cards.body: It's the same trick from Level 9: time turned into distance. So what exactly are you counting toward?

cards.headline: A storm's three ingredients
cards.body: A thunderstorm needs three things. Moisture, usually from the ocean. Unstable air: warm, moist air near the ground with cold, dry air above it. And lift, a nudge that gets the warm air rising, such as a mountain slope or colliding air. Once the air is rising, the cloud grows taller and taller, with strong updrafts and downdrafts inside. Moisture, instability, lift: bake at high altitude.

mascot.line: Five times hotter than the Sun, for a split second. Lightning does not do things halfway.

cards.headline: Lightning and thunder
cards.body: Lightning is a huge electrical discharge between clouds, or from a cloud to the ground. It heats its narrow channel of air to as much as 30,000°C, about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. Air that hot expands violently, and that blast is thunder. You see the flash almost instantly, but the sound takes about 3 seconds to travel 1 km. Hence the counting.

cards.headline: Tornadoes: storms that touch down
cards.body: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air that reaches from a thunderstorm down to the ground. The strongest ones usually come from supercells, big thunderstorms whose winds are already rotating. The United States has more tornadoes than any other country, most of them on the central plains east of the Rocky Mountains. Great country for storm chasers. Less great for trampolines.

title: Climate Zones
objective: After this level you can name the main climate zones and say where on Earth each one occurs.
summary: Köppen sorted climates by the plants they grow into five groups: tropical near the Equator, dry deserts about 15 to 30 degrees out, temperate, continental interiors and polar.

cards.headline: The ancient Greeks sorted the world's climates with Level 4's lines.
cards.body: They split the world into five zones: a torrid zone between the tropics, two temperate zones, and two frigid zones beyond the polar circles. Not bad for a first draft.

cards.headline: Köppen's map, drawn by plants

What grows in a place depends on its temperature and rainfall, so Köppen drew his climate borders to match the zones of vegetation. The plants had been mapping climate all along; he just read their map. He sorted the world into five main groups: tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar. Here's where each one lives.

title: A Changing Climate
objective: After this level you can explain the greenhouse effect and how Earth's climate is changing today.
summary: Greenhouse gases keep Earth livable by trapping heat. Burning fossil fuels has raised CO2 by more than 50%, and Earth has warmed about 1°C, mostly because of us.

cards.headline: Without greenhouse gases, Earth would average about -18°C.
cards.body: Instead it averages about 15°C. So the greenhouse effect isn't the villain of this story. Too much of it is.

cards.headline: A blanket made of gas
cards.body: Sunlight warms Earth's surface, and the surface gives off heat. Gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapor trap some of that heat near the surface, like a blanket on a cold night. That's the greenhouse effect, and it's what keeps the planet from freezing. The trouble starts when you keep adding blankets.

cards.headline: We've thickened the blanket
cards.body: Since industrial times began in the 1700s, carbon dioxide in the air has risen by more than 50%, mainly from burning coal, oil and gas. Earth's average surface temperature has climbed about 1°C since the late 1800s. That sounds small, but it's the whole planet's average, and today's warming is roughly 10 times faster than the average warming after an ice age. Human activity is the main cause.
cards.callout: More greenhouse gas, more trapped heat.

mascot.line: Weather is one page. Climate is the whole diary. And the diary keeps getting warmer.

cards.headline: Weather or climate? Level 31 again
cards.body: A cold snap in a warming world is still weather. Blizzards and freezing days keep happening; over time they happen less often. Climate change shows up in the long-term averages, and those are climbing. Global sea level, for one, rose about 20 cm in the last century, and it's rising faster now. One chilly week can't argue with a century of data.

title: Checkpoint: Climate and Weather
objective: After this level you can explain how sunlight, wind, water and mountains combine to make weather and climate.
summary: The Hadley cell ties the chapter together: sunlight lifts air at the Equator, which rains; the dried air sinks near 30 degrees, making deserts, and returns as the trade winds.

cards.headline: Rainforest at the Equator, desert near the tropics. One loop of air does both.
cards.body: You already know the pieces: Level 32's sunshine, Level 33's winds, Level 34's rising and sinking air. Time to snap them together.

cards.headline: Up at the Equator
cards.body: Direct sunlight heats the air near the Equator, and up it goes, like Level 33's hot-air balloon. As it rises it cools and drops its moisture as heavy rain, which is why the Equator is so rainy. The air, now wrung dry, spreads out toward the poles, high in the sky.

cards.headline: Down near 30 degrees
cards.body: Around 30° north and south, that dry air sinks and warms up again. Sinking air blocks clouds from forming, just like on Level 34's leeward slopes, so little rain falls and deserts like the Sahara form. Then the air flows back toward the Equator along the ground, bent by the Coriolis effect. That return flow is the trade winds. Loop closed.

mascot.line: Sun, wind, rain and desert, all in one loop. That is a whole chapter in a single breath of air.

cards.fact: George Hadley proposed this loop in 1735 to explain the trade winds.
cards.context: The loop now carries his name: the Hadley cell. It links nearly everything in this chapter. Sunlight makes the heat, pressure makes the wind, rising air makes the rain, and sinking air makes the deserts.

title: What Is a Biome?
objective: After this level you can explain what a biome is and how climate shapes it.
summary: A biome is a large area defined by its plants, soil, climate and wildlife. Temperature and rain decide which biome grows where, so similar climates grow lookalike landscapes.

cards.headline: Five places, oceans apart, wearing the same outfit.
cards.body: California, Chile, South Africa, southern Australia and the lands around the Mediterranean are scattered across the globe. Yet all five share the same kind of climate, and the same kind of scrubby hillsides. Coincidence? Not even slightly.

cards.headline: What a biome is
cards.body: A biome is a big region defined by its plants, soil, climate and wildlife. Biomes are usually named after their main plants, like grassland or coniferous forest. They come in five major types: forest, grassland, desert, tundra and aquatic. That last one is the watery one, and its marine part, which includes the ocean and coral reefs, covers close to three-quarters of Earth's surface. Think of biomes as the planet's neighborhoods. This chapter visits them one by one.
cards.callout: Forest · Grassland · Desert · Tundra · Aquatic

mascot.line: Two dials, a whole planet of landscapes. Not bad for a thermostat and a rain gauge.

cards.headline: Two dials: heat and rain
cards.body: So what decides which biome you get? Mostly climate. A simple way to sort biomes is by two dials: temperature and precipitation. Keep it hot and wet all year and you get rainforest. Turn the rain way down and you drift into desert. And wherever the same biome turns up on the planet, it comes with similar kinds of plants and animal life. Same settings, same neighborhood.

cards.fact: Those five lookalike scrublands are full of plants that aren't closely related.
cards.context: What they share is a climate of mild, wet winters and long, dry summers. In each region, different ancestor plants developed similar features to cope with it, a process called convergent evolution. California calls its version chaparral; South Africa has fynbos. Same climate, same costume, different actors inside.

title: Rainforests
objective: After this level you can describe tropical rainforests and explain why they hold so many species.
summary: Tropical rainforests grow in the tropics, warm and wet all year. Built in four layers, they cover a small slice of Earth yet hold more than half of its plant and animal species.

cards.headline: Noon in the rainforest. Bring a flashlight.
cards.body: The tropical Sun is blazing overhead, yet down on the forest floor it's dim. On average only about 2% of the sunlight makes it all the way down. Something up there is catching nearly all of it.

cards.headline: A forest with four floors
cards.body: Most rainforests are built in four layers. The tallest trees, the emergents, poke out on top. Below them spreads the canopy, then the dim understory, and at the bottom the forest floor. Between them, the upper layers soak up almost all the light, which makes the floor the darkest layer, a place where plants struggle to grow. It's less one forest than four stacked on top of each other.

cards.headline: Summer that never ends
cards.body: Tropical rainforests grow mainly in the tropics, between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn you met in Level 4. Temperatures stay high and rain is plentiful all year, with little change from season to season. No winter shutdown, no dry spell. Plenty of sunlight and moisture are the building blocks for a huge variety of plants and animals, and the rainforest never runs short of either.

mascot.line: Tiny footprint, packed guest list. Remember this trick: it turns up again under the sea.

cards.fact: Rainforests cover a small slice of Earth, yet hold more than half of its plant and animal species.
cards.context: Sources put that slice at only about 2 to 6% of Earth's surface. The biggest of them all is the Amazon, the world's largest tropical rainforest. If all of Earth's species threw one party, more than half the guests would be squeezed into a few small rooms.

title: Deserts
objective: After this level you can explain why deserts form and why not all of them are hot.
summary: A desert is defined by dryness, not heat. Belts of sinking dry air near 30° latitude and mountain rain shadows make deserts, and the largest of all is icy Antarctica.

cards.headline: The world's largest desert is covered in ice.
cards.body: Not the Sahara, which is the largest hot desert. The biggest desert of all is Antarctica. If that sounds like a trick question, it's because we picture deserts as hot and sandy. The real test has nothing to do with heat.

cards.headline: The only rule: dryness
cards.body: A desert is simply a place that gets very little precipitation. Some experts set the limit at about 250 mm a year, less than the length of a school ruler. Temperature doesn't come into it. A scorching dune field and a frozen plain can both qualify, as long as the sky stays stingy.

cards.headline: Where the sky is a lid
cards.body: Many big deserts sit in belts around 30° to 35° north and south of the Equator, just outside the tropics from Level 4. In those belts, dry air sinks from high up, bringing clear skies and very little rain. The Sahara, the largest hot desert on Earth, lies in one of them. Clouds rarely stand a chance.

mascot.line: One side gets the rain, the other gets the shadow. Mountains are terrible at sharing.

cards.headline: Mountains that steal the rain
cards.body: Mountains make deserts too. As moist air climbs a range, it cools, and clouds drop rain and snow on the way up. By the time the air slides down the far side, it's warming and its clouds fade away. That dry side is a rain shadow. Death Valley, in California and Nevada, is so dry because it sits in the rain shadow of the Sierra Nevada.

cards.fact: Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth.
cards.context: Its interior gets only about 50 mm of precipitation a year, almost all of it snow. The air there is so cold that it holds very little water vapor, so there's hardly anything to fall. A continent buried in ice, and bone dry.

title: Grasslands and Savannas
objective: After this level you can describe grasslands and savannas and the animals they support.
summary: Grasslands grow where there is too little rain for forest but too much for desert. Savannas add scattered trees and a long dry season, and fire and grazing keep both open.

cards.headline: Mow it, graze it, burn it. Grass comes back.
cards.body: Your lawn after the mower is a tiny lesson in one of Earth's toughest biomes. A grass leaf grows from its base, at or below ground level, safely out of harm's way. Keep that trick in mind.

cards.headline: The land in between
cards.body: Grasslands fill the gap between forests and deserts. They get too little regular rain to grow a forest, but not so little that a desert forms. You'll find them on every continent except Antarctica, under different local names: prairie in North America, steppe across Asia and Eastern Europe, pampas in South America. Same biome, many passports.
cards.callout: Prairie · Steppe · Pampas · Savanna

cards.headline: Savanna: grass with a few trees
cards.body: A savanna is a grassland dotted with scattered trees. It stays warm to hot all year, but the rain comes in only a few months, and the dry season is usually the longer one. The largest savannas are in Africa. That's where the African elephant roams, the largest animal on land, strolling through what is basically a very big, very sunny lawn.

mascot.line: A plant that thrives on being eaten and burned. Grass has a very relaxed attitude to disaster.

cards.headline: Why the trees don't take over
cards.body: Give a grassland a run of wet, quiet years and woody plants start creeping in. Drought, fire and heavy grazing push back, and all three favor grass. On savannas, wildfires stop woody plants from spreading. Grass shrugs it off: when fire or grazers strip its leaves, it regrows from its base, using energy stored in its roots. Fire isn't the grassland's enemy. It's the gardener.

title: Forests of the North
objective: After this level you can describe temperate and northern forests and how they survive winter.
summary: Winter makes water scarce. Deciduous trees drop their leaves, revealing yellows hidden all summer; conifers keep waxy needles instead, and rule the taiga, the largest land biome.

cards.headline: Every autumn, some trees throw away all their leaves. On purpose.
cards.body: Their evergreen neighbors keep theirs all winter. Two opposite strategies for the same enemy, and that enemy isn't only the cold.

cards.headline: Winter is a drought
cards.body: In winter, much of the water is locked up as ice, so it's in short supply, and a plant with no way to save water would dry out. Deciduous trees solve it bluntly. Before winter, a special layer of cells grows where each leaf's stem meets the tree and cuts the leaf loose. Bare branches aren't a sign of giving up. They're a tree battening down the hatches.

mascot.line: All summer long, the gold was hiding in plain sight. Trees are very good at secrets.

cards.headline: The yellow was there all summer
cards.body: As fall days shorten and cool, leaves stop making food and their green chlorophyll breaks down. Underneath, yellow and orange pigments were there all along, hidden by the green. Reds and purples are different: those come from anthocyanin pigments that form in the fall. So when a tree turns gold, it isn't putting on a new color. It's taking off its green coat.

cards.headline: Needles: the evergreen answer
cards.body: Conifers like pine, spruce and fir take the other route and keep their leaves. Their needles are built to save water: a small surface for their size, sunken pores and a thick, waxy coating. Their shape helps as well, because snow slides off the peaks of cone-shaped trees instead of piling up. They're dressed for winter all year.

cards.fact: The taiga, or boreal forest, is the largest land biome on Earth.
cards.context: It's a belt of cone-bearing evergreens circling the far north, across Canada and Alaska and on through Russia. Winters there are long and very cold, and a lasting snowpack is the norm. Tundra lies to its north, and temperate forest to its south.

title: Tundra
objective: After this level you can describe the tundra and the frozen ground beneath it.
summary: The tundra is treeless land over permafrost, ground frozen for years. Only a thin top layer thaws in summer, so meltwater is trapped and the land turns soggy.

cards.headline: The tundra gets little rain. So why are your boots soaked?
cards.body: Walk across the Arctic tundra in summer and the ground squelches. The land is a patchwork of wet spots, even though very little falls from the sky. The answer is buried right under your feet.

cards.headline: The land without trees
cards.body: The word tundra comes from a Finnish word for a barren or treeless hill, and that's exactly the look: small shrubs, grasses, mosses, sedges and lichens, all hugging the ground. Arctic tundra lies on land above the Arctic Circle from Level 4, at about 66.5° N. Alpine tundra lies high on mountains, where nights drop below freezing.

cards.headline: Frozen for years
cards.body: Beneath the Arctic tundra lies permafrost: ground that stays frozen for at least two years. In summer, only a thin layer at the surface thaws. Everything below it stays frozen solid, like a freezer with the lid cracked open a little.

mascot.line: Water on top, ice underneath, nowhere to go. The tundra is one giant puddle with a frozen floor.

cards.headline: A frozen floor under a wet rug
cards.body: That frozen layer works like a waterproof floor under the thin soil. Meltwater can't soak down through it, so it stays trapped near the surface. That's why the tundra is dotted with wet ground even though it gets little precipitation. Mystery of the soggy boots: solved.

cards.fact: Only six to ten weeks a year are warm enough for tundra plants to grow.
cards.context: That's far too short a season for plants that grow wood. Strong winds dry out and batter whatever sticks up, and permafrost stops roots from reaching deep enough to hold a tree upright. So tundra plants stay small and low.

title: Climbing Through Climates
objective: After this level you can explain how climate and life change as you climb a mountain.
summary: Air cools about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m you climb, so a tall tropical mountain stacks climates like a trip toward the poles, as Humboldt saw on Chimborazo in 1802.

cards.headline: Climb one mountain and cross a whole planet's worth of climates.
cards.body: In 1802, Alexander von Humboldt climbed Chimborazo, a volcano in Ecuador about one degree south of the Equator. He started among tropical plants in the valleys and ended up near the snow line, among lichens. He'd walked from the Equator toward the poles without leaving one mountain.

cards.headline: Colder with every step up
cards.body: Near Earth's surface, air gets cooler the higher you climb: on average about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m. So a tall mountain is a stack of climates, warm at the bottom and cold at the top. Remember Level 7's Everest, about 8,849 m above sea level? Its summit is the top floor of the tallest building on Earth, and the heating is definitely off up there.
cards.callout: Up 1,000 m ≈ down 6.5 °C

cards.headline: Humboldt's big picture
cards.body: Humboldt didn't reach Chimborazo's summit, but his climb stood as a mountaineering record for nearly 30 years. What he brought down mattered more. The plant zones stacked up the mountain, from tropical valleys to lichens near the snow, matched the zones you'd pass on a journey from the Equator toward the poles. In 1807 he published a famous cross-section drawing of the mountain, with each plant placed at the height where it grew.

mascot.line: Up is a bit like north. Mountains are just shortcuts to the Arctic.

cards.headline: Where the trees give up
cards.body: Keep climbing and you reach the timberline, the upper limit of tree growth. Where it sits depends largely on temperature. Above it you find alpine tundra, Level 46's treeless land lifted onto a mountaintop. The same limit shows up at high latitudes, like the Arctic. Go up far enough, or north far enough, and trees run out of warmth.

cards.fact: Humboldt's plant zones have moved more than 500 m uphill.
cards.context: In 1802 he found seed plants up to about 4,600 m on Chimborazo, with only lichens above. When researchers retraced his survey in 2012, they found plants growing as high as 5,185 m. The main reason: a warming climate. The zones are still stacked, just on a higher shelf.
