title: Coral Reefs
objective: After this level you can explain what coral reefs are and why they are so fragile.
summary: Corals are animals that partner with food-making algae. Reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean yet hold nearly a quarter of its species, and water that is too warm makes them bleach.

cards.headline: Earth's biggest structures made by life are built by nickel-sized animals.
cards.body: A coral polyp is soft, and most are no thicker than a nickel. But each one builds a hard limestone skeleton, and together they build coral reefs, the largest structures made by living things.

cards.headline: Animal, not plant
cards.body: Corals stay put, fixed to the seafloor like plants, but they're animals: they can't make their own food the way plants do. So they take in lodgers. Tiny algae called zooxanthellae live inside the coral's tissue. The coral gives them a home, and the algae use sunlight to make food and share it. They're the coral's main food source. Rent, paid in lunch.

cards.fact: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean, yet nearly a quarter of all ocean species live there.
cards.context: Reef-building corals grow in clear, warm, moving water in tropical and subtropical seas, where sunlight can reach their algae. Sound familiar? Level 42's rainforests pull the same trick on land: a small slice of Earth holding more than half of its plant and animal species.

mascot.line: Kicking out the roommate who buys all the groceries. Bold move, coral.

cards.headline: Why a coral turns white
cards.body: When the water gets too warm, stressed corals expel the algae living in their tissues and turn completely white. That's coral bleaching. Those algae were the coral's main food and its color, so a bleached coral isn't dead yet, but it's starving. If the stress eases, it can recover. If the heat goes on, it eventually dies.

title: Wetlands
objective: After this level you can explain what wetlands do for water and wildlife.
summary: Wetlands are land where water covers or soaks the soil for at least part of the year. They soak up floods like sponges, clean water like kidneys and shelter a big share of wildlife.

cards.headline: The soggiest land around may be the hardest working.
cards.body: It soaks up floods, cleans dirty water and gives fish and birds a place to raise their young. It just doesn't look very impressive while doing it. Meet the wetland.

cards.headline: Land that's partly water
cards.body: A wetland is any place where water covers the soil, or sits at or near the surface, all year or for part of it. The plants tell you which kind you're standing in. Marshes are ruled by grasses and other soft, non-woody plants. Swamps are dominated by woody plants: shrubs or trees. Grass means marsh. Trees mean swamp. Wet socks mean either.
cards.callout: Marsh: grasses · Swamp: shrubs and trees

cards.headline: A sponge for floods
cards.body: Wetlands act as natural sponges. They trap rain, snowmelt, groundwater and floodwater, then let it go slowly. Picture pouring a bucket of water onto a kitchen counter, and then onto a big sponge. The counter sends it all straight onto the floor. The sponge takes it in and gives it back a little at a time.

cards.headline: The kidneys of the watershed
cards.body: Wetlands clean water too. They hold it still long enough for sediment and other pollutants to settle out, and they filter out excess nutrients. That's why they've been called the kidneys of our watersheds. Water leaves cleaner than it arrived, and nobody even sends a bill.

mascot.line: Sponge, filter and nursery in one. Not bad for a puddle with ambitions.

cards.fact: More than a third of US threatened and endangered species live only in wetlands.
cards.context: Nearly half use wetlands at some point in their lives. Most commercial and game fish breed in coastal marshes and estuaries, and ducks, geese, hawks, wading birds and many songbirds nest in wetlands. Drain a swamp and you evict a crowd.

title: Milestone: The Physical World
objective: After this level you can connect landforms, water, climate and biomes into one picture of how Earth works.
summary: Earth works as connected systems: rock, water, air and life (plus ice). A breeze crossing a mountain shows them all at work, from rain to rain shadow to the biome on each side.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Time to see the physical world in one picture.
cards.body: You mapped the planet in Chapter 1 and toured its biomes in this one. Now zoom out. Rock, water, air and life aren't separate stories. They're parts of one machine.

cards.headline: Four spheres, one planet
cards.body: Scientists split Earth into connected systems. The geosphere is rock, from the crust down to the core. The hydrosphere is water, and Level 1 showed it covers about 71% of the surface. The atmosphere is the envelope of gas around us. The biosphere is all life. Many add a fifth, the cryosphere, for ice. And all of them constantly interact.
cards.callout: Geosphere · Hydrosphere · Atmosphere · Biosphere

mascot.line: Rock, water, air and life, all in one weather report. Earth is a team sport.

cards.headline: One breeze, every sphere
cards.body: Watch them team up. Moist air (atmosphere) climbs a mountain range (geosphere) and drops rain and snow on the way up (hydrosphere). The far side, starved of water, sits in a dry rain shadow. Which biome grows on each slope (biosphere) depends on how much heat and rain it gets. One breeze, and every sphere has a part to play.

title: Africa in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe Africa's size and how its landscapes change from north to south.
summary: Africa is the second-largest continent. The Equator cuts it almost in half, so its climates are mirrored: rainforest in the middle, then savanna, desert and Mediterranean tips.

cards.headline: Three famous lines of latitude cross Africa. No other continent gets all three.
cards.body: The Equator, the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn from Level 4 all run through it. That's a clue to how big Africa is, and to how its landscapes are laid out.

cards.headline: Bigger than your map admits
cards.body: Africa is the second-largest continent, after Asia, and covers about one-fifth of Earth's land. Your wall map probably undersells it. Remember Level 2: Africa is about 14 times bigger than Greenland, yet on a Mercator map they look like rivals. Mercator inflates places far from the Equator, and the Equator cuts Africa almost exactly in half. Greenland gets the boost. Africa doesn't.

mascot.line: Fold Africa along the Equator and its climates nearly line up. Geography's neatest party trick.

cards.headline: A continent folded in half
cards.body: With the Equator through its middle, Africa's climates copy themselves on each side, like a folded inkblot. Wet rainforest sits in the center. Move north or south and it opens into savanna, grassland with scattered trees. Farther out come the deserts: the Sahara in the north, the Kalahari and the Namib in the south. At the far tips, north and south, you'll find Mediterranean climates.
cards.callout: Rainforest › savanna › desert › Mediterranean, in both directions

cards.fact: Savanna covers almost half of Africa.
cards.context: So the safari picture of grass and scattered trees isn't a postcard cliché. It's the most typical Africa there is. The mirror isn't perfect, though: thanks to the bulge of western Africa, more of the continent lies north of the Equator than south of it.

title: The Sahara
objective: After this level you can describe the Sahara and how it has changed over thousands of years.
summary: A desert is defined by low precipitation, so Antarctica is the largest desert; the Sahara is the largest hot one and mostly rock. About 11,000 years ago it was green.

cards.headline: People once went fishing in the middle of the Sahara.
cards.body: Not at an oasis. On the shores of real lakes, in a place that's now some of the driest land on Earth. To see how, start with what a desert actually is.

cards.headline: Desert means dry, not hot
cards.body: A desert is land that gets no more than about 25 cm of precipitation a year. Heat and sand are optional. By that rule, the largest desert on Earth is Antarctica, the icy continent from Level 1. The Sahara, across northern Africa, is the largest hot desert, almost the size of the contiguous United States. Big enough to swallow a country, and still only the runner-up.

cards.fact: Most of the Sahara isn't sand.
cards.context: Sand dunes cover only a minority of it. The rest is rocky plateaus and gravel plains. The movie version, golden dunes rolling to the horizon, is real, but it's the exception. Much of the world's most famous sandy place is closer to an endless stony parking lot.

mascot.line: Hippos in the Sahara. Somewhere, a very confused camel is reading this over your shoulder.

cards.headline: The green Sahara
cards.body: About 11,000 years ago, the Sahara was green, with lakes, rivers and grasslands. People painted what they saw on its rocks: elephants, giraffes, rhinos, hippos. The cause was a slow wobble of Earth's axis, which shifted summer sunlight, strengthened the African monsoon and pushed its rains north. Then the rains retreated, and the Sahara dried out between about 8,000 and 4,500 years ago.

title: The Nile
objective: After this level you can explain how the Nile made farming and cities possible in Egypt.
summary: The Nile flows north to the Mediterranean. Its yearly flood, driven by the Blue Nile, left black silt that let Egypt farm a desert, until the Aswan High Dam in 1970.

cards.headline: About 95% of Egyptians live within a few miles of one river.
cards.body: Draw a thin line along the Nile and you've circled almost the whole country's population. For thousands of years, that river did something a desert shouldn't allow: it made farmland.

cards.headline: A river that runs up the map
cards.body: The Nile, usually ranked the world's longest river, flows north, into the Mediterranean Sea. It has two main branches. The longer White Nile starts at Lake Victoria; the Blue Nile starts near Lake Tana in Ethiopia. They meet at Khartoum, in Sudan. The Blue Nile is the shorter branch, but it's the one that matters most: it brings the annual flood and most of the water and silt.

cards.headline: Black land, red land
cards.body: Each year the flood spread fertile silt over the valley, and farming became possible in the middle of a desert. Egyptians named their country for it: Kemet, the 'black land.' The desert beyond was Deshret, the 'red land.' Where the river reaches the sea, all that silt built the rich Nile Delta, the triangle-shaped plain named for the Greek letter Δ back in Level 7.

cards.fact: Since 1970, the Nile hasn't flooded Egypt.
cards.context: That year the Aswan High Dam was completed, and the annual flood ended. The dam's steady flow lets farmers irrigate all year. The catch: the silt that once fed the fields now builds up behind the dam. Egypt traded a free yearly delivery of fertilizer for control.

title: The Great Rift Valley
objective: After this level you can explain how the Great Rift Valley formed and why it matters to the story of human origins.
summary: Africa is splitting along the East African Rift as the Somali plate pulls away; the Red Sea is a rift already flooded. Rift fossils like Lucy, dated by volcanic ash, tell the human story.

cards.headline: Africa is splitting in two.
cards.body: Slowly: you won't feel it, and nobody alive will see the ending. But in East Africa the ground is being pulled apart, and the scar it leaves holds some of the oldest chapters of the human story.

cards.headline: A valley made by pulling
cards.body: The river valleys of Level 7 were carved by water and ice. The Great Rift Valley was made by pulling. In the East African Rift, the Somali plate, carrying the Horn of Africa, is moving away from the Nubian plate. As they separate, they stretch and thin the crust between them, and the rift opens. The system runs from the Middle East to Mozambique, dotted with volcanoes.

cards.fact: The Red Sea is a rift that the ocean already flooded.
cards.context: Arabia was once joined to Africa. Then the two rifted apart and the ocean poured into the valley between them. East Africa may be on the same path: someday the sea could flood the rift and make the Horn of Africa an island. Not for millions of years, so no need to cancel any trips.

mascot.line: A volcano that erupts on schedule would be nice. Settling for one whose ash keeps good time.

cards.headline: Where the oldest bones turn up
cards.body: The rift is one of the best places on Earth to find early human relatives. Lucy, a 3.2-million-year-old skeleton of a species that walked upright, came from Ethiopia. Turkana Boy, 1.5 million years old, came from Kenya. The rift helps twice. Layers of volcanic ash can be dated, which dates the fossils between them. And at places like Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, running water cuts through the layers and exposes the bones.

title: Kilimanjaro and Africa's Peaks
objective: After this level you can describe Africa's highest mountains and their shrinking ice.
summary: Kilimanjaro, a volcano about 3° south of the Equator, rises 5,895 m as Africa's highest point. Its ice, and Mount Kenya's, is shrinking; Kilimanjaro has lost more than 85% since 1912.

cards.headline: In 1848, a man saw snow near the Equator. It wasn't believed for over a decade.
cards.body: Johannes Rebmann had seen a snow-capped mountain in East Africa. He was right. The mountain was Kilimanjaro, and today the story is how fast that snow and ice are going.

cards.headline: Africa's rooftop
cards.body: Kilimanjaro, in Tanzania, rises 5,895 m above sea level: the highest point in Africa. It's one of the volcanoes that dot the Great Rift Valley from Level 54. And it stands only about 3° south of the Equator, deep in the tropics, which is exactly why snow up there sounded so ridiculous in 1848.

cards.fact: Kilimanjaro's summit ice has lost more than 85% of its mass.
cards.context: That's between 1912 and 2011. Warming is only part of the story. The region's air has grown drier, which means less fresh snow to rebuild the ice and fewer clouds to shade it from the Sun. Scientists estimate the ice could vanish by 2060.

mascot.line: First nobody believed the ice was there. Now it may not be there to believe in. Tough crowd, glaciers.

cards.headline: The Equator's other ice
cards.body: Kilimanjaro isn't alone. Mount Kenya, Africa's second-highest mountain, sits just south of the Equator and still has small glaciers. They're retreating, too. So the snow near the Equator that Rebmann's readers doubted turned out to be real. It's just running out.

title: The Congo Basin

summary: The Congo Basin holds the world's second-largest rainforest. The Congo River crosses the Equator twice, so part of its basin is always rainy and it flows steadily.

cards.headline: There is an ape that lives on only one side of one river.
cards.body: Bonobos live only along the south bank of the Congo River. The river runs through a forest so big that only the Amazon's is bigger.

cards.headline: Africa's green heart
cards.body: Remember Level 51's folded map, with wet rainforest in the middle? The biggest block of it is the Congo Basin: the world's second-largest rainforest, after the Amazon. The Equator runs straight through it, and so does the river that drains it, the Congo.

cards.headline: The river that crosses the Equator twice
cards.body: The Congo River swings through the forest in a giant arc and crosses the Equator twice. That odd route is its secret. Its basin spans both sides of the Equator, so some part of it is always in its rainy season, and the river flows steadily all year. Only the Amazon carries more water.

cards.fact: Bonobos live only on the Congo River's south bank.
cards.context: They're found in the lowland rainforest of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and nowhere else in the wild. For you, the Congo is a line on a map. For a bonobo, it's the edge of the world.

title: Africa's Countries and Cities
objective: After this level you can name Africa's most populous countries and largest cities.
summary: Africa has 54 countries, more than any continent; Algeria is the largest and Nigeria the most populous. It is the youngest continent, and its big cities include Cairo, Lagos and Kinshasa.

cards.headline: About 19% of the world's people live in Africa. Half are under about 19.
cards.body: Africa has the world's youngest population, with a median age of about 19. Picture a continent where the typical person is still choosing a college major.

cards.headline: Fifty-four pieces
cards.body: Africa is split into 54 recognized countries, more than any other continent. The largest is Algeria, and the Sahara from Level 52 makes up more than four-fifths of it. Algeria only took the title in 2011, when South Sudan split off from Sudan, the old champion. The country with the most people is Nigeria.

cards.headline: Cities on the water
cards.body: Cairo, Lagos and Kinshasa are among Africa's largest cities. Cairo stands on the Nile, at the gateway to Level 53's delta. Lagos is Nigeria's largest city, though not its capital: that moved to Abuja in 1991. And Kinshasa sits on the Congo River, with a surprising neighbor.

cards.fact: Two capital cities face each other across the Congo River.
cards.context: Kinshasa, capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, is on one bank. Brazzaville, capital of the Republic of the Congo, is on the other. No bridge links them, so boats carry people between two countries' capitals. Your commute has nothing on that.

title: The Middle East
objective: After this level you can locate the Middle East and describe its deserts, rivers and seas.
summary: The Middle East is a loosely defined region centered on Southwest Asia. Much of it is desert, but the Tigris and Euphrates water Mesopotamia, and the Dead Sea is Earth's lowest land.

cards.headline: The lowest land on Earth is a shore where swimmers float with no effort.
cards.body: It's the edge of the Dead Sea, more than 400 m below sea level. Getting there means crossing a region full of deserts and rivers.

cards.headline: A region without a border
cards.body: The Middle East has no official border. It's a loosely defined region centered on Southwest Asia, often stretched to include Egypt. Large parts of it are desert. The Arabian Peninsula holds the Rub' al Khali, the Empty Quarter: the world's largest area of continuous sand. After Level 52's mostly rocky Sahara, here is the endless dune sea you pictured.

cards.headline: The land between the rivers
cards.body: Two rivers break the dry spell. The Tigris and Euphrates rise in the mountains of Turkey and flow southeast toward the Persian Gulf. The land between them is Mesopotamia, Greek for 'between rivers,' mostly in modern Iraq. Its soil is fertile but rain is scarce, so farming there depended on irrigation from the rivers. It's the Nile's bargain from Level 53, told with two rivers.

mascot.line: I tried to swim a lap there once. I mostly floated in a slow, salty circle.

cards.fact: The Dead Sea's shores are the lowest land on Earth.
cards.context: The water lies more than 400 m below sea level, and it keeps dropping as the water that fed it is diverted. The Jordan River flows in and nothing flows out, and the water is so salty and dense that swimmers float easily. It sits in a down-dropped block of crust along a major plate boundary.

title: Oil and Water
objective: After this level you can explain why oil and fresh water shape life in the Middle East.
summary: The Persian Gulf countries hold about half the world's proved oil reserves, but the region has very little fresh water, so Gulf countries burn oil and gas to desalinate the sea.

cards.headline: Kuwait has no rivers or lakes. So it drinks the sea.
cards.body: The country sits in one of the driest regions on Earth, on top of one of its richest resources. The trick of this level is how the second solves the first.

cards.headline: Half the world's oil, around one gulf
cards.body: The seven countries around the Persian Gulf hold about half of the world's proved crude oil reserves. That oil began as tiny plants and animals in ancient seas. Buried under sand, silt and rock, they were cooked by heat and pressure into crude oil. The land on top is bone dry. The rock underneath is loaded.

cards.fact: The region has about 6% of the world's people and less than 2% of its fresh water.
cards.context: That's the Middle East and North Africa. Remember Level 1: about 71% of Earth's surface is water. The catch: about 96.5% of Earth's water is in the oceans, too salty to drink. The region is surrounded by water it can't use as it comes.

mascot.line: Oil and water don't mix, they say. In the Gulf, one keeps the taps running for the other.

cards.headline: Trading oil for water
cards.body: So the Gulf makes its own. Desalination removes the salt from seawater, and Kuwait gets about 90% of its drinking water that way. It takes a lot of energy, and the Gulf countries power it with oil and natural gas. The fuel under the sand turns the sea into something you can drink.

title: Checkpoint: Africa and the Middle East
objective: After this level you can describe the main landscapes, rivers and resources of Africa and the Middle East.
summary: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, links the Mediterranean and Red Seas without locks, separates Africa from Asia and lets ships skip the long voyage around Africa.

cards.headline: In 1869, ships got a shortcut that let them skip a whole continent.
cards.body: Before it, a ship sailing between Europe and Asia had to go all the way around Africa. Afterward it could cut through Egypt. The shortcut ties together almost everything in this chapter.

cards.headline: Sea to sea, no locks
cards.body: The Suez Canal connects the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea. It needs no locks, because the two seas sit at about the same level. And remember where the Red Sea came from: Level 54's rift, where Arabia pulled away from Africa and the ocean flooded in. Cut across one narrow neck of land, and an ancient crack in the crust becomes a shipping lane.

mascot.line: Left window: Africa. Right window: Asia. Best continental view you can get without leaving your seat.

cards.headline: A line between continents
cards.body: The canal is also a border. It separates Africa from Asia, so Egypt's Sinai Peninsula, east of the canal, lies in Asia. Just west of it spreads the Nile Delta, the silt-built farmland from Level 53. Ships sliding through have Africa on one side and Asia on the other, and they save the whole trip around Africa's Cape of Good Hope.

title: Europe in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe Europe's shape, seas and main regions.
summary: Europe is the western peninsula of Eurasia, bordered by the Urals and three bodies of water. It's a peninsula of peninsulas, with four physical regions running north to south.

cards.headline: Europe and Asia share one piece of land. So where does one end?
cards.body: No ocean splits them. Walk east from Paris and no sea blocks your way into Asia. The line between the two continents is one that people chose.

cards.headline: The western tip of Eurasia
cards.body: Europe and Asia share one great landmass, Eurasia, and Europe is its western peninsula. The border between them is usually drawn along Russia's Ural Mountains: a line on the map, not a gap in the ground. Level 8 ranked Europe second smallest of the seven continents, ahead of only Australia. Small, but wrapped in water on three sides: the Arctic Ocean to the north, the Atlantic to the west and the Mediterranean Sea to the south.

mascot.line: A peninsula made of peninsulas. It's peninsulas all the way down.

cards.headline: A peninsula of peninsulas
cards.body: Land with water on three sides is a peninsula, and Europe keeps repeating the trick. Geographers sometimes call it a peninsula of peninsulas. Look at a map and the big ones jump out: the Scandinavian in the north, then the Iberian, the Italian and the Balkan along the south. Europe is basically a coastline with a continent attached.
cards.callout: Scandinavian · Iberian · Italian · Balkan

cards.headline: Four stripes, north to south
cards.body: Inland, Europe falls into four bands. In the north and west are the Western Uplands: hard, ancient rock scraped by glaciers, which left lakes and fjords behind. Next comes the North European Plain, low land running from the southern UK to Russia and Europe's most densely populated region. Then the Central Uplands, heavily wooded, stretching across central Europe. Last, in the south, the Alpine Mountains: the Alps, Pyrenees, Apennines and Carpathians. Keep that southern stripe in mind. Next level, we climb it.

title: The Alps and Europe's Rivers
objective: After this level you can explain how the Alps and rivers like the Rhine and Danube shaped Europe.
summary: The Alps are fold mountains pushed up by a fragment of the African plate. Their water feeds rivers flowing to four seas, including the Rhine, and the Danube crosses 10 countries.

cards.headline: Snow melting in the Alps can end up in four different seas.
cards.body: The North Sea, the Mediterranean, the Adriatic or the Black Sea. One mountain range, four destinations. Europe's great rivers start up here.

cards.headline: Europe's crumpled edge
cards.body: The Alps are the centerpiece of Level 61's southern stripe, arcing from the Mediterranean coast near Nice, France, to Vienna, Austria. They're fold mountains: they form where tectonic plates are pushed together and rock crumples upward, like a rug shoved against a wall. Here the pusher is the Adriatic microplate, a fragment of the African plate, driving into Eurasia. The top of the crumple is Mont Blanc, the highest peak in the Alps.

cards.headline: Europe's water tower
cards.body: All that height collects snow, and the meltwater has to go somewhere. The Alps are the source of the Rhône, the Rhine and the Po, plus many of the Danube's tributaries. The Rhine rises in the Swiss Alps and runs north and west to the North Sea, draining through the Netherlands. Along the way it has become one of the world's most important routes for industrial transport: less a river, more a conveyor belt with a view.

mascot.line: Mountains split the water; a canal gets it back together. I love a reunion story.

cards.fact: The Danube passes through 10 countries.
cards.context: It rises in Germany's Black Forest and rolls east to the Black Sea, Europe's second-longest river after the Volga. The capitals Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade all stand on its banks. Since 1992, the Main-Danube Canal has linked it to the Main, a Rhine tributary, so boats can travel between the North Sea and the Black Sea. The Alps send Europe's water in four directions. Engineers joined two of them back up.

title: The Mediterranean
objective: After this level you can explain the Mediterranean's climate and why the sea connected ancient peoples.
summary: The Mediterranean lies between Europe, Africa and Asia. Its climate brings hot, dry summers and cool, wet winters, and ancient seafarers settled all around its shores.

cards.headline: Socrates had a picture for his world: frogs around a pond.
cards.body: In Plato's Phaedo, he says the people living between the Pillars of Hercules and the river Phasis live around the sea like ants or frogs around a pond. The pond was the Mediterranean. The frogs were busy.

cards.headline: The sea in the middle of the land
cards.body: Mediterranean comes from Latin words meaning "in the middle of the land", and the name fits. Europe, Africa and Asia wrap around it. It meets the Atlantic Ocean through the Strait of Gibraltar, about 13 km wide at its narrowest. And those Pillars of Hercules? They're the two headlands at the strait's eastern end. The pond has a front gate.

cards.headline: Hot, dry summers; cool, wet winters
cards.body: Around the pond, the weather follows a pattern famous enough to borrow the sea's name: the Mediterranean climate. Summers are hot and dry, and winters are cool and wet. The reason is a summer visitor. A subtropical high-pressure system spreads over the region, bringing sinking air, clear skies and heat. Find the same climate elsewhere between about 30° and 45° latitude, on the western sides of continents.

mascot.line: Croak if you founded a colony. Very loud pond, the ancient Mediterranean.

cards.headline: A pond, not a wall
cards.body: For ancient peoples, this sea was a road. Greek seafarers founded colonies all along the coasts, from Spain and France to Italy, North Africa and the Black Sea. Trade usually came first, and many colonies became trading hubs. The Greeks didn't have the water to themselves, either: the Phoenicians and Etruscans founded colonies too. Hence the frogs. Plenty of neighbors, one shared pond.

title: Russia, the Biggest Country
objective: After this level you can describe Russia's size, Siberia and its eleven time zones.
summary: Russia is by far the largest country, but most Russians live in its European part. Siberia covers about three-quarters of Russia, and the country spans 11 time zones.

cards.headline: Board a train in Moscow and you'll reach Vladivostok about seven days later.
cards.body: It's the Trans-Siberian, the longest single rail system in the world, and the trip spans eight time zones. You never leave the country. Pack snacks. Lots of snacks.

cards.headline: The biggest country, by far
cards.body: Russia is by far the world's largest country. It stretches across all of northern Asia and the eastern third of Europe, split by the Ural Mountains that Level 61 used as the usual border between the two continents. Yet its people bunch up at one end: most Russians live in the European part, especially around Moscow. Huge house, and everyone's in the front room.

cards.headline: Siberia: most of the map
cards.body: East of the Urals lies Siberia, running all the way to the Pacific Ocean, and from the Arctic Ocean south to Kazakhstan, Mongolia and China. In its wider sense it covers about three-quarters of Russia. It's sparsely settled, and swampy forest called taiga covers most of it. The winters are serious: in the Sakha region, temperatures as low as −68 °C have been recorded. Your freezer is a tropical getaway by comparison.

cards.headline: Eleven clocks, one country
cards.body: All that width shows up on the clock. Russia spans 11 time zones, from Kaliningrad on the Baltic Sea to Kamchatka on the Pacific. Remember Level 5: Earth turns 15° of longitude every hour, so each zone covers a slice of about that width. Kaliningrad and Kamchatka are 10 hours apart. When it's 9:00 a.m. in Kaliningrad, it's 7:00 p.m. in Kamchatka. Breakfast at one end, dinner at the other.

title: Asia in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe Asia's regions and why most people on Earth live there.
summary: Asia, the largest continent, holds about three-fifths of the world's people. They crowd into South Asia, eastern China and the Pacific coasts, while the interior stays nearly empty.

cards.headline: About three in every five people on Earth live in Asia.
cards.body: Yet huge stretches of Asia are almost empty. Both are true at once. The trick is where people choose to live.

cards.headline: One continent, many neighborhoods
cards.body: Asia is the giant from Level 8, holding almost a third of the world's land. That's too much to take in at once, so geographers divide it into regions: East Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Central Asia, West Asia and North Asia. North Asia is Siberia, the frozen forest you crossed in Level 64. Same continent, very different neighborhoods.

cards.headline: Crowded here, empty there
cards.body: Asia's people aren't spread evenly. Vast areas of Central and North Asia have stayed sparsely populated because their climates are forbidding. Instead, people are concentrated in the Indian subcontinent, the eastern half of China, the Pacific borderlands and the islands. A population map of Asia looks like a party where everyone is standing by the windows.

mascot.line: Save me a seat at that table. Near the dumplings, ideally.

cards.fact: About 90% of the world's rice is grown and eaten in Asia.
cards.context: Grown there and eaten there: the same continent does both. When about three in five people share one continent, it takes a lot of rice to fill the bowls. Next time you order fried rice, you're joining a very long dinner table.

title: The Himalayas
objective: After this level you can describe the Himalayas, Mount Everest and the great rivers they feed.
summary: India's collision with Asia crumpled the crust into the Himalayas, lifting old seafloor to Everest's summit. The range still rises, and its snow feeds great rivers.

cards.headline: The top of Mount Everest used to be the bottom of a sea.
cards.body: The rocks near the summit are limestone laid down on the floor of an ancient sea, the Tethys, and they hold fossils of sea creatures. Today they sit about 8,849 m above sea level. Something lifted a seabed onto the world's highest mountain.

cards.headline: India's slow-motion crash
cards.body: The lifter was India. It drifted north and collided with Asia about 40 to 50 million years ago. The two had about the same rock density, so neither plate could slide under the other. With nowhere else to go, the crust was thrust upward, seabed and all, into the Himalayas. They're fold mountains, like the Alps in Level 62, with the Indian plate as the pushy neighbor.

cards.fact: The Himalayas are still rising, by more than 1 cm a year.
cards.context: The crash isn't over. The Indian plate is still pushing north into the Eurasian plate, squeezing the range like a very slow press. Your fingernails grow faster, but the Himalayas have had millions of years of practice.

mascot.line: Seafloor to summit, then snow back to sea. Rocks have the longest commutes.

cards.headline: The abode of snow
cards.body: Himalaya comes from Sanskrit words meaning "abode of snow", and all that snow and ice feeds rivers. The Himalayas are drained by 19 major rivers, and the Indus and the Brahmaputra are the largest. The Ganges begins here too, as a stream flowing out of the Gangotri Glacier. Mountains built from an old seabed now send their water back toward the sea.

title: China's Great Rivers
objective: After this level you can explain how the Yangtze and the Yellow River shaped China.
summary: The silt-laden Yellow River is the cradle of Chinese civilization and 'China's Sorrow'. The Yangtze is Asia's longest river, home to nearly a third of China's people.

cards.headline: China has a river named after the color of its mud.
cards.body: The Yellow River, Huang He in Chinese, gets its name from the fine yellow silt called loess that it carries to the sea. That mud explains both of its nicknames.

cards.headline: Cradle and sorrow
cards.body: The Yellow River is often called the cradle of Chinese civilization. It also earned a darker nickname, "China's Sorrow", for its destructive floods. Picture a relative who helped raise you but also, now and then, floods the kitchen. Both reputations come from the same place: the mud.

cards.headline: A river above the fields
cards.body: Remember Level 7's deltas, built from sediment a slowing river drops? The Yellow River does the same thing along its bed. Over time that sediment has built the bed up above the surrounding land in many places; even at low water it can sit about 5 m above the countryside. People built extensive levees to hold it in, yet the river has changed its course across the plain several times. A river on a raised shelf has a long way to fall.

mascot.line: The Long River. Named by someone who clearly walked the whole thing.

cards.fact: The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia.
cards.context: At about 6,300 km, it's the third longest in the world, and its Chinese name, Chang Jiang, simply means "Long River". It rises in the Tanggula Mountains on the Tibetan Plateau and flows to the East China Sea. Its basin is China's great granary and home to nearly one-third of the country's people. Some names don't need a poet.

title: India and South Asia
objective: After this level you can describe South Asia's landscapes, its monsoon and its huge population.
summary: South Asia is a subcontinent walled off by the Himalayas. The summer monsoon brings about three-quarters of India's rain, and India is now the most populous country.

cards.headline: In India, about three-quarters of a year's rain arrives in one season.
cards.body: When that season delivers, harvests boom. When it fails, crops can fail too. Meet the monsoon.

cards.headline: A subcontinent behind a wall
cards.body: India, Bangladesh and most of Pakistan form a subcontinent, set off from the rest of Asia by the Himalayas from Level 66. India's land falls into three big pieces: the Himalayas in the north, the Deccan plateau in the south, and the Indo-Gangetic Plain between them. The Ganges crosses that plain through one of the most fertile and densely populated regions in the world.

mascot.line: Summer: the sea breathes in on the land. Winter: the land breathes back out.

cards.headline: Winds that switch sides
cards.body: Monsoon comes from the Arabic mawsim, "season", and that's the whole idea: a major wind system that reverses direction with the seasons. Land heats and cools more than the ocean, so monsoon winds usually blow from sea to land in summer and from land to sea in winter. India's summer monsoon, from about mid-June to early October, carries moist air in from the Indian Ocean and brings about three-quarters of the year's rain.

cards.fact: In 2023, India overtook China as the world's most populous country.
cards.context: That's according to the United Nations. Feeding so many people leans on one season of rain. Good monsoon years bring bumper crops; poor rains can mean crop failure, especially where there's no irrigation. In South Asia, a weather forecast is also a harvest forecast.

title: Islands of Fire
objective: After this level you can explain why Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines have so many volcanoes and earthquakes.
summary: Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines lie on the Ring of Fire, a belt around the Pacific with about 75% of Earth's volcanoes. Subduction, one plate diving under another, makes the magma.

cards.headline: Japan has 111 active volcanoes. That's about a tenth of the world's.
cards.body: Indonesia and the Philippines rumble too. Three island countries, one reason: they sit on the same ring.

cards.headline: A ring around the Pacific
cards.body: The Ring of Fire is a horseshoe-shaped belt around the Pacific Ocean, about 40,000 km long, lined with volcanoes and frequent earthquakes. About 75% of Earth's volcanoes lie along it, and most earthquakes happen along it too. Trace it on a map and it runs right through Japan, the Philippines and Indonesia. They aren't unlucky. They're on the route.

cards.headline: Where one plate dives under another
cards.body: Along much of the ring, plates meet at subduction zones, where one plate is pushed down beneath another. The sinking rock helps melt rock into magma, which can rise and erupt. Japan shows the recipe at full strength: it sits where four plates meet (the Pacific, Philippine Sea, Eurasian and North American), and its volcanoes formed largely along subduction zones. The planet recycles its floor, with fireworks.

title: Checkpoint: Europe and Asia
objective: After this level you can describe the main mountains, rivers and regions of Europe and Asia.
summary: The Alpide belt runs from the Atlantic through the Mediterranean and the Himalayas to Indonesia. Continents crumple into fold mountains along it, and in Indonesia it meets the Ring of Fire.

cards.headline: One restless line runs from the Atlantic all the way to Indonesia.
cards.body: It passes the Mediterranean and the Himalayas, and it shakes. This chapter has been following it without saying so.

cards.headline: The Alpide belt
cards.body: Geologists call it the Alpide belt. It runs from the Atlantic through the Mediterranean region and the Himalayas to Java and Sumatra in Indonesia. Its mountains are the Alpine-Himalayan ranges: Level 62's Alps and Level 66's Himalayas are two beads on the same string. It's restless, too, producing about 17% of the world's largest earthquakes.

cards.headline: Crumple or dive
cards.body: Along this belt, plates push into Eurasia: a fragment of Africa behind the Alps, India behind the Himalayas. When continents meet like India and Asia, their rock has about the same density, so neither plate can slide under the other and the crust crumples upward. Compare Level 69's Ring of Fire, where one plate dives beneath another and helps make magma. Crumple, and you get fold mountains. Dive, and you get volcanoes.

mascot.line: Two earthquake belts shaking hands. Firmly. Very firmly.

cards.fact: In Indonesia, the Alpide belt meets the Ring of Fire.
cards.context: Two of the planet's great earthquake belts join up in one island country. Remember Level 69's volcanic zone running from Sumatra through Java? That's where this chapter's line finally reaches the Pacific's ring. Busy neighborhood.

title: North America in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe North America's regions from the Arctic to Central America.
summary: North America runs from near the North Pole almost to the Equator: Canada, the US, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, with mountains on both edges and plains in between.

cards.headline: One continent nearly touches the North Pole and nearly reaches the Equator.
cards.body: North America stretches to within about 800 km of both. Planning a trip from one end to the other? Pack a parka, pack sunscreen, and bring a very big suitcase.

cards.headline: Three giants and a bridge
cards.body: Most of the land belongs to three big countries: Canada, the United States and Mexico. Canada alone is the second-largest country on Earth. South of Mexico, the continent narrows into Central America, seven countries in a row, and the Caribbean islands sit just offshore. Greenland counts as North American, too, and it's the largest island in the world.

cards.headline: Old in the middle, tall in the west
cards.body: Picture the continent as neighborhoods of different ages. At its core sits the Canadian Shield, a stable platform of very ancient rock. In the east rise the old Appalachian Mountains. In the west rise the younger, much taller Cordilleras, which cover nearly a third of the land. Between the two mountain belts lies a huge, mostly flat middle of plains. Mountains on both edges, flat in the center: keep that shape in mind. This whole chapter lives in it.

cards.fact: Most of North America lies between the Arctic Circle and the Tropic of Cancer.
cards.context: Two of Level 4's lines make neat bookends. And in Level 8's ranking, North America is the third-largest continent, behind only Asia and Africa. A bronze medal, but a very roomy one.

title: The Rockies and the Great Plains
objective: After this level you can explain how the Rockies and the Great Plains divide the continent.
summary: The Rockies run from Canada to New Mexico, and along their crests the Continental Divide splits Pacific water from Atlantic-side water. East of them, the Great Plains slope gently down.

cards.headline: In the Rockies, one ridge decides which ocean a raindrop reaches.
cards.body: Two raindrops land a step apart on a mountain crest. One heads for the Pacific. The other drains toward the Atlantic side. Same storm, different oceans.

cards.headline: The backbone of the West
cards.body: Remember Level 71's tall western mountains? The Rocky Mountains are the most famous of them. They stretch some 4,800 km, from northern Alberta and British Columbia in Canada all the way south to New Mexico. That's a very long wall to build a road over, and a very long wall for rain to land on.

mascot.line: A raindrop never gets to choose. It just picks a side of the roof and hopes for the best.

cards.headline: The roof of a continent
cards.body: Along the Rockies runs the Continental Divide, a ridge that separates the continent's river systems. Rain that falls west of it drains toward the Pacific. Rain that falls east of it heads for the Atlantic and Arctic Oceans and the Gulf of Mexico. Think of the ridge of a roof: which side a drop lands on decides which gutter it ends up in.

cards.headline: A tilted sea of grass
cards.body: East of the Rockies, the land flattens into the Great Plains, stretching from the Rio Grande all the way north to the Mackenzie River delta on the Arctic Ocean. Flat, but not level: at the foot of the mountains the plains sit about 1,500 to 1,800 m above sea level, then slope gently down to about 460 m in the east. Rain is scarce and wind is plentiful, so grass, not forest, covers the land. A ramp so gentle you'd never notice you were driving downhill.

title: The Mississippi
objective: After this level you can explain how the Mississippi river system drains the middle of North America.
summary: The Mississippi starts as a wadeable stream at Lake Itasca, drains about 40% of the continental US, collects Rocky Mountain water via the Missouri and builds a delta on the Gulf.

cards.headline: You can wade across the Mississippi. Just once, right at the start.
cards.body: At Lake Itasca in Minnesota, the great river begins as a shallow, knee-deep stream, and visitors splash from one bank to the other. Try that farther downstream and you'll want a boat. A big one.

cards.headline: A funnel for 31 states
cards.body: From Itasca, the Mississippi flows about 3,766 km south to the Gulf of Mexico. Along the way it collects water from an enormous area: all or part of 31 US states and 2 Canadian provinces, about 40% of the continental US. Picture a kitchen funnel as wide as the middle of the continent. The Mississippi is the spout.

cards.headline: Water from the Rockies
cards.body: Big branches pour in from both sides: the Ohio from the east and the Missouri from the west. The Missouri, the Mississippi's longest tributary, begins in the Rocky Mountains of Montana. Remember Level 72's raindrop, the one that landed just east of the Continental Divide? It can ride the Missouri into the Mississippi and on to the Gulf of Mexico. Same drop, extremely long trip.

mascot.line: A river is a delivery service. The delta is where it finally drops off the packages.

cards.fact: The Mississippi ends in a vast delta southeast of New Orleans.
cards.context: It's Level 7's landform on a giant scale. A delta is flat, low land built at a river's mouth from the sediment the slowing river drops. The Mississippi hauls mud from a huge share of the continent, and near the sea it finally sets its load down.

title: The Great Lakes
objective: After this level you can describe the Great Lakes and how glaciers carved them.
summary: Five lakes, Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario, hold about 21% of the world's surface fresh water. Glaciers scoured and deepened their basins, and their water drains east to the Atlantic.

cards.headline: Five lakes hold about 21% of the world's surface fresh water.
cards.body: Split all the fresh water on the world's surface into five equal glasses, and the Great Lakes would fill one of them by themselves. That's a lot of water for one corner of one continent.

cards.headline: Meet HOMES
cards.body: The five Great Lakes are Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario. Shuffle their first letters and you get HOMES, the classic way to remember them. Four are shared by the US and Canada; Lake Michigan is the only one entirely inside the US. Together they hold 84% of North America's surface fresh water. Every other lake and river on the continent splits the leftovers.

cards.headline: Dug by ice
cards.body: Where did such giant holes come from? Starting about a million years ago, massive glaciers pushed through the middle of the continent. They scoured existing valleys, widening and deepening them into the basins the lakes now fill. It's Level 7's glacier trick on a giant scale: rivers cut V-shaped valleys, and ice grinds them wider. The glaciers were the diggers. The lakes are what they left behind.

cards.headline: A different door to the sea
cards.body: The lakes aren't a dead end. Their water flows east through the St. Lawrence River into the Atlantic Ocean. Compare that with Level 73's Mississippi, which carries the water south of them all the way to the Gulf of Mexico. Close neighbors on the map, but they leave for the ocean by different doors.

title: The Grand Canyon
objective: After this level you can explain how the Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon.
summary: The land was lifted into the Colorado Plateau, then the Colorado River spent 5 to 6 million years cutting down through it, exposing rocks nearly 2 billion years old at the bottom.

cards.headline: A river dug a hole more than a mile deep.
cards.body: The Grand Canyon in Arizona drops about 1,800 m below its rim and runs about 446 km long. No bulldozers were involved. Just one river and a lot of patience.

cards.headline: Step one: lift the land
cards.body: Before a river can dig a deep canyon, it needs something tall to dig into. Between about 70 and 30 million years ago, the whole region was pushed upward into the Colorado Plateau, high and fairly flat. That's Level 7's plateau: flat land raised up high. The higher the land, the farther down a river can cut.

mascot.line: Moving water plus gritty sand plus millions of years. Slow, but it never takes a day off.

cards.headline: Step two: saw it open
cards.body: Then the Colorado River got to work. Starting 5 to 6 million years ago, it began carving downward. Water alone isn't much of a cutter, but the river carries sand and rocks, and those do the grinding, like sandpaper dragged across the riverbed again and again. Grain by grain, the river sawed through the plateau. The water is the saw; the sand is its teeth.

cards.fact: The oldest rocks at the canyon bottom are nearly 2 billion years old.
cards.context: Rock layers stack up like a pile of newspapers: the oldest at the bottom, newer ones on top. The layer at the rim is about 270 million years old, a youngster by comparison. So a hike down into the Grand Canyon is a walk back in time, one layer per chapter.

title: Mexico and Central America
objective: After this level you can describe the volcanoes, highlands and coasts of Mexico and Central America.
summary: Plates meet under Mexico and Central America, so volcanoes are everywhere. Mexico's heartland is a high plateau, and Central America is a narrow isthmus with a wet Caribbean coast.

cards.headline: In 1943, a volcano was born in a farmer's cornfield.
cards.body: On February 20, the ground in Dionisio Pulido's field in Mexico cracked open and started throwing out ash. The new volcano, Parícutin, kept erupting for 9 years. Definitely not the crop he planted.

cards.headline: Volcano country
cards.body: Mexico is volcano country. An active volcanic belt crosses central Mexico, and its peaks include Citlaltépetl (also called Orizaba), a volcano that is Mexico's highest point. Farther south, some 40 volcanic cones line Central America's Pacific side. The cause is underground: several of Earth's plates meet here and press on each other, so the ground shakes and volcanoes grow.

cards.headline: Life on the high table
cards.body: Between two long ranges, the Sierra Madre Occidental in the west and the Sierra Madre Oriental in the east, lies the Mexican Plateau. It's Mexico's largest and most densely populated region. Near its southern end, around Mexico City, the land rises about 2,100 to 2,700 m above sea level. Mexico's heartland isn't a coastal plain; it's a high tabletop between mountains.

mascot.line: An isthmus is just a land bridge with a fancy name. Try saying it three times fast.

cards.headline: A bridge between continents
cards.body: South of Mexico, the land narrows into Central America, an isthmus that links North and South America. At its narrowest, in Panama, it's only about 50 km wide. Its two coasts don't get the same weather, either: the Caribbean side receives about twice as much rain as the Pacific side. Two oceans, one short drive apart.

title: The Caribbean
objective: After this level you can describe the Caribbean islands and explain their hurricane season.
summary: The Caribbean islands curve in a long crescent, led by Cuba. Hurricanes feed on warm water, so the season runs June to November and peaks in September, when the sea is warmest.

cards.headline: Hurricane season has a start date and an end date.
cards.body: In the Atlantic, it officially runs from June 1 to November 30. Storms can't read calendars, so why does the season keep to one? The answer is floating all around the Caribbean islands.

cards.headline: A crescent of islands
cards.body: The Caribbean islands, also called the West Indies, curve in a crescent more than 3,200 km long, fencing off the Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico from the open Atlantic. The big ones, Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica and Puerto Rico, form the Greater Antilles, and Cuba is the largest of all. Hispaniola is one island shared by two countries, Haiti and the Dominican Republic. The smaller Lesser Antilles curve away to the southeast like a trail of stepping stones.

cards.headline: Hurricane fuel
cards.body: A hurricane is a rotating storm that forms over tropical or subtropical waters, and its fuel is warm ocean water: at least 26.5°C. Those warm seas are Level 4 territory: the tropics, the only places where the Sun ever stands directly overhead. Warm tropical water is the fuel tank, and a hurricane is the engine that burns it.

cards.headline: Why not June?
cards.body: If the Sun is strongest in late June, why doesn't hurricane season peak then? Because oceans warm slowly. It takes several weeks after the Sun's peak for the sea to reach its warmest, just as a summer day is hottest in mid-afternoon, not at noon. So the season peaks around September 10, with most activity from mid-August to mid-October.

title: South America in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe South America's regions and largest countries.
summary: South America has 12 independent countries, and Brazil covers about half of it. The Andes run down the west, the Amazon basin fills the north, and the continent tapers south to Patagonia.

cards.headline: One South American country is named after a line on the map.
cards.body: Ecuador is Spanish for equator, and the Equator runs right through it. Level 4's imaginary line, the one that splits the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, got a whole country named after it.

cards.headline: Twelve countries and one giant
cards.body: South America has 12 independent countries, plus French Guiana, which is part of France. One of them dominates: Brazil covers about half the continent's land and borders every other South American country except Chile and Ecuador. Brazilians speak Portuguese, while Spanish is the main language in most of the rest. So Brazil is less a neighbor than the whole neighborhood.

cards.headline: A shape you can draw
cards.body: Sketch the continent and you'll draw a wide top that tapers to a point in the south. The Andes run down the entire western edge. The vast Amazon basin fills the north. Broad plains and lowlands spread through the east and center, and Patagonia stretches across the far south. Mountains in the west and flatter land to the east: sound familiar? Level 71's North America has tall western mountains and a flat middle, too.

cards.fact: South America is the fourth-largest continent.
cards.context: In Level 8's ranking, it comes right after North America. Most of it lies in the tropics, yet its narrow southern tail reaches all the way to subantarctic latitudes. Pack for both, again.

title: The Amazon and the Andes
objective: After this level you can explain how the Andes and the Amazon shape South America.
summary: The Andes, the longest continental range, carry the Continental Divide down South America's west. The Amazon rises near the Pacific but flows east to the Atlantic with a fifth of Earth's runoff.

cards.headline: The Amazon starts about 160 km from the Pacific. It ends in the Atlantic.
cards.body: Imagine a river that begins a short drive from one ocean and then crosses a whole continent to reach the other one. The mountains decided the route, and Level 72 already told you how.

cards.headline: The longest mountain wall
cards.body: The Andes are the world's longest continental mountain range, running along South America's western edge through seven countries. Their highest peak, Aconcagua, on the border of Argentina and Chile, is the highest point in the Western Hemisphere. And Level 72's Continental Divide doesn't stop in the Rockies: it runs through Mexico and Central America and right down the Andes.

mascot.line: Every fifth drop running off the land, anywhere on Earth, is riding the Amazon. Busy river.

cards.headline: So the water goes east
cards.body: The Amazon rises high in the Andes of Peru, on the side that drains away from the Pacific, then flows east across the whole continent to the Atlantic. Along the way it gathers so much water that it carries about one-fifth of all the water that runs off Earth's surface. One river, a fifth of the planet's runoff. That's a lot of rain finding the same exit.

cards.fact: The Amazon drains the largest river basin in the world.
cards.context: It's the biggest river system both by the area it drains and by the water it carries. Remember Level 73's Mississippi funnel, draining about 40% of the continental US? The Amazon's funnel is bigger still. Same idea, larger kitchen.

title: Checkpoint: The Americas
objective: After this level you can describe the main mountains, rivers and regions of North and South America.
summary: The Pan-American Highway runs Alaska to Argentina, broken only by the Darién Gap. The Continental Divide follows the western mountains, and big rivers drain the land east of them.

cards.headline: You can drive from Alaska to the tip of South America. Almost.
cards.body: One road network runs nearly 30,600 km down both continents, and there's exactly one place where it stops cold. Let's take the trip anyway, with everything from this chapter in the glovebox.

cards.headline: Follow the spine
cards.body: The Pan-American Highway runs from Alaska and Canada all the way to the southern tip of Argentina. For the whole trip, a mountain spine keeps you company: the Continental Divide, which runs from western Alaska along the Rockies, through Mexico and Central America, and down the Andes. Two continents, one long rooftop.

mascot.line: All that road, and the missing piece is exactly where the continents meet. Classic.

cards.fact: The only break is the Darién Gap: about 100 km of roadless rainforest.
cards.context: It lies between Panama and Colombia, exactly where Level 76's narrow isthmus joins North America to South America. So the one road built to link the two continents stops right at the seam between them.

cards.headline: Mountains west, rivers east
cards.body: Step back and both continents share a design. Tall mountains line the west, and giant rivers drain the land east of them. The Mississippi runs south to the Gulf of Mexico, fed by the Missouri from the Rockies. The Amazon flows east from the Andes to the Atlantic. Same blueprint, drawn twice.

title: Australia in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe Australia's dry interior and explain where most Australians live.
summary: Australia is the smallest continent but one of the largest countries. Most of it is arid Outback, so more than 8 in 10 Australians live near the coast, mostly in the east.

cards.headline: Australia is a whole continent. Most Australians live on its edges.
cards.body: More than 8 in 10 of them live within 50 km of the sea. A population map looks like a picture frame: a busy border around an almost empty middle. So what's wrong with the middle?

cards.headline: Last among continents, near the top among countries
cards.body: Remember Level 8's ranking? Australia came last: the smallest continent, and the flattest, too. Now look at it as a country, and it's one of the largest on Earth. Same land, two league tables, and it lands at opposite ends of them.

cards.fact: Except for Antarctica, Australia is the driest continent.
cards.context: Around 70% of the land is arid or semi-arid. That dry heart has a name, the Outback: a vast, flat interior with very few people. It covers most of the map but holds very few people. The picture frame starts to make sense.

cards.headline: Life on the rim
cards.body: So Australians hug the coast, and most of them live along the east coast, where the coastal rim is more fertile. Behind those eastern cities runs the Great Dividing Range, a line of mountains along the Pacific coast that separates them from the Outback. For most Australians, the beach isn't a holiday destination. It's the neighborhood.

title: Uluru and the Outback
objective: After this level you can describe the Outback and what Uluru means to Aboriginal Australians.
summary: Uluru rises 348 m from the Outback plain, the tip of a much bigger buried slab, red with rusting iron. It is sacred to the Anangu, who own it; the climb closed in 2019.

cards.headline: A rock in the Outback is taller than the Eiffel Tower. That's just the tip.
cards.body: Most of it is hidden underground. And the part you can see has been sacred to the people who own it for tens of thousands of years.

cards.headline: A buried giant
cards.body: Level 81's dry, flat, nearly empty interior is the Outback. In the Outback of the Northern Territory, one rock rises 348 m above the surrounding plain: Uluru. That's taller than the Eiffel Tower. Yet Uluru and its neighbor Kata Tjuta are only the tips of huge rock slabs that carry on underground for up to 6 km. You're looking at the top of a buried giant.

mascot.line: Next time your bike rusts, tell it that it's going for the Uluru look.

cards.headline: A rock that rusts
cards.body: Uluru is made of arkose, a kind of sandstone with iron in it. Over time that iron rusts, just like an old bike left out in the rain, and the rust is Uluru's famous red. In grey patches you can see the rock's original color. So the most famous red rock in Australia is, underneath, a grey one wearing a coat of rust.

cards.headline: Whose rock?
cards.body: Uluru belongs to the Aṉangu, its Traditional Owners. It has been sacred to them for tens of thousands of years, and under Tjukurpa, Aṉangu law and culture, climbing it was generally not allowed. In 1985 the park was handed back to Aṉangu, who lease it to the Australian Government and run it jointly with Parks Australia. On 26 October 2019 the climb closed for good. Visitors now admire Uluru the way its owners always asked: from the ground.

title: The Great Barrier Reef
objective: After this level you can describe the Great Barrier Reef and the threats it faces.
summary: The Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, was built by colonies of tiny polyps. Warm water makes corals bleach, and climate change is its greatest threat.

cards.headline: The biggest coral reef system on Earth was built by animals.
cards.body: Not by rocks or waves. By tiny creatures living in colonies, adding one skeleton at a time. And right now, those builders are in trouble.

cards.headline: Builders that become the building
cards.body: A coral isn't a plant or a rock. It's made of animals called polyps. Hard corals build skeletons of calcium carbonate, and a colony can hold hundreds to hundreds of thousands of polyps, all cemented together. Colony on colony, skeleton on skeleton, a reef grows. It's a city where the bricklayers are also the bricks.

cards.fact: The Great Barrier Reef stretches more than 2,000 km off northeastern Australia.
cards.context: It's the world's largest coral reef system, made of nearly 3,000 individual reefs. It grows in the Coral Sea, part of the Pacific, the biggest ocean from Level 8. The biggest ocean holds the biggest reef.

mascot.line: White coral is a warning light, not a gravestone. The question is how long the warning lasts.

cards.headline: Why corals turn white
cards.body: Corals share their bodies with tiny algae, which are their main food source and give them their color. When the water gets too warm, stressed corals expel the algae and turn white. That's bleaching. A bleached coral isn't dead yet: it can recover if the stress eases, but if it drags on, the coral dies. That's why the reef's managers name climate change as its greatest threat.

title: New Zealand
objective: After this level you can explain how moving plates shaped New Zealand's mountains and hot springs.
summary: New Zealand straddles the Australian and Pacific plates. In the South Island they push up the Southern Alps; in the North Island the Pacific Plate slides under, feeding volcanoes and geysers.

cards.headline: New Zealand's highest mountains and its geysers share one cause.
cards.body: Two of Earth's plates meet right under the country. On one island they shove mountains upward. On the other, they heat the groundwater until it erupts as geysers.

cards.headline: A country on a seam
cards.body: New Zealand sits across the boundary between two tectonic plates: the Australian Plate and the Pacific Plate. Off the North Island the boundary lies under the sea, but in the South Island it comes ashore. You can see it on land as the Alpine Fault, the line where the two plates meet. Here you can walk right up to a seam in the planet.

mascot.line: Up a little, worn down a little, every single year. Now that's commitment.

cards.headline: Mountains on an escalator
cards.body: Along the Alpine Fault, the Pacific Plate pushes upward and builds the Southern Alps. They rise about 7 mm a year, but erosion wears them down at a similar rate. It's like walking up a down escalator: lots of effort, not much gain. The highest peak, Aoraki/Mount Cook, stands at 3,724 m.

cards.headline: Hot water in the north
cards.body: In the North Island the plates meet differently: the Pacific Plate slides under the Australian Plate, and deep down, rock melts. Some of that molten rock erupts from volcanoes such as Ruapehu. Some stays underground and heats the water in the rocks. That's what powers the geysers and hot springs around Rotorua and Taupō. Same two plates, a different move, and completely different scenery.

The plate keeps moving and carries each island away, so the chain gets older toward the northwest. At the young end sits the island of Hawaii. At the old end sits Kure Atoll: no volcano in sight, just a ring of coral.

Finally the island vanishes under the sea, and only the ring of reef is left around a lagoon: an atoll. In the 1950s, scientists drilled into Enewetak Atoll, went through more than 1 km of coral and hit volcanic rock. The volcano had been down there all along.

title: Wayfinders of the Pacific
objective: After this level you can explain how Polynesian navigators crossed the Pacific by reading stars, waves and birds.
summary: Polynesian wayfinders crossed the Pacific without instruments, using where stars rise and set, ocean swells and homing seabirds. Hokulea's 1976 voyage to Tahiti proved it could be done.

cards.headline: In 1976, a canoe sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti with no compass and no charts.
cards.body: Its navigator, Mau Piailug, used no instruments at all. The map was in his head, and the clues were all around him.

cards.headline: A triangle of ocean
cards.body: Draw a triangle with corners at Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island (Rapa Nui). That's Polynesia. People settled it in large sailing canoes, on long voyages that began roughly 3,000 to 4,000 years ago. So how do you find a speck of land in all that water, with nothing but your eyes?

cards.headline: A compass made of stars
cards.body: Wayfinders memorize where each star rises and sets on the horizon. Watch a known star come up and you know your direction, no magnet required. Hawaiian navigators call this a star compass. And when the Sun climbs too high to steer by, they read the sea instead and steer by the ocean swells.
cards.callout: Stars for direction, swells for steering

cards.headline: Follow the birds home
cards.body: Near land, the ocean starts dropping hints. Seabirds like terns fly out to sea in the morning to fish and head back to land in the late afternoon. Spot them flying home and you can simply follow them. Swells bending around an island and clouds piling up over it give land away, too, long before you can see it.

cards.fact: Hōkūleʻa's 1976 voyage showed the Pacific could be settled on purpose.
cards.context: Some people thought Polynesians had reached their islands by accidental drift. Mau Piailug, a navigator from Satawal in Micronesia, guided the canoe to Tahiti by the old methods, and more than 17,000 people turned out to welcome it. The old way worked.

title: The Arctic
objective: After this level you can describe the Arctic Ocean and its shrinking sea ice.
summary: The Arctic is an ocean ringed by continents, capped with sea ice that peaks in March and bottoms out in September. The September ice is shrinking about 12% per decade.

cards.headline: Stand at the North Pole and there's no land under your boots.
cards.body: Just frozen ocean. And since satellites started watching in 1979, the late-summer ice has been shrinking by about 12% every decade.

cards.headline: An ocean with a lid
cards.body: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by continents. It's the smallest of the five oceans, and right over the North Pole it wears a lid of floating sea ice. So the North Pole isn't a spot on land at all. It's a point on a frozen sea. Planting a flag there is more like planting it on a raft.

cards.headline: Ice that breathes
cards.body: Sea ice is simply frozen ocean water: it forms, grows and melts in the sea. Through the winter the Arctic's ice spreads out, usually reaching its biggest extent in March. Through the summer it shrinks, usually hitting its smallest in September. Watch a year of satellite maps and the Arctic seems to breathe in and out.

mascot.line: White shirt in summer, every time. The Arctic has been telling us this for years.

cards.fact: September's Arctic sea ice is shrinking about 12% per decade.
cards.context: The loss feeds itself. Sea ice reflects 50 to 70% of the sunlight that hits it, but darker open ocean reflects only 6% and soaks up the rest. So less ice means more heat in the water, which means even less ice. It's the difference between wearing a white T-shirt and a black one on a sunny day.

title: Antarctica
objective: After this level you can explain why Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent.
summary: Antarctica's ice sheet holds about 90% of the world's ice and makes it the highest continent. Height helps make it the coldest; so little snow falls that it's a desert.

cards.headline: Antarctica is buried in ice. It's also a desert.
cards.body: It's the highest, driest, windiest, coldest and iciest continent on Earth. One giant ice sheet explains a surprising amount of that list.

cards.headline: A continent wearing a mountain of ice
cards.body: Antarctica is a rocky continent capped by an ice sheet up to 4.8 km thick, holding about 90% of all the ice on Earth. All that ice lifts the surface so high that Antarctica is the highest continent, averaging about 2,200 m above sea level. In a sense, much of Antarctica's height is made of frozen water.

cards.fact: The coldest temperature ever measured on Earth: −89.2 °C.
cards.context: It was recorded at Vostok station in Antarctica on 21 July 1983. Height is part of the reason. Air gets colder the higher you go, and Antarctica sits higher on average than any other continent. Antarctica is cold partly for the same reason mountaintops are.

mascot.line: So the biggest pile of frozen water on Earth sits in a desert. Geography loves a plot twist.

cards.headline: Dry as a desert, windy as an open freezer
cards.body: A desert is defined by how little precipitation falls, usually less than about 250 to 500 mm a year, not by heat. Antarctica's snowfall adds up to only about 150 mm of rain a year, so it's a cold, dry desert. And the wind? Air over the ice cools, gets heavier and pours downhill toward the coast. These katabatic winds are like the cold air spilling out of an open freezer, only continent-sized.

title: Who Owns Antarctica?
objective: After this level you can explain the Antarctic Treaty and what it protects.
summary: Seven countries claim parts of Antarctica, some overlapping. The 1959 Antarctic Treaty freezes those claims and keeps the continent for peace and science; the Madrid Protocol bans mining.

cards.headline: Seven countries claim slices of Antarctica. Three of the slices overlap.
cards.body: It looks like a pie cut by squabbling relatives. So who's actually in charge down there? A deal struck in 1959 has the answer.

cards.headline: Seven slices of pie
cards.body: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the United Kingdom all claim parts of Antarctica. On the Antarctic Peninsula, the claims of Argentina, Chile and the United Kingdom overlap, so the same patch of ice is claimed three times over.

cards.headline: Freeze the argument
cards.body: On 1 December 1959, twelve countries active in Antarctica signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington. It came into force in 1961. Its clever move was to not settle who owns what. Instead, it holds the old claims in place and forbids any new or bigger claim while the treaty lasts. The argument isn't won. It's put in the freezer, which in Antarctica is fitting.

cards.headline: Peace and science only
cards.body: The treaty says Antarctica shall be used for peaceful purposes only: no military bases, no maneuvers, no weapons tests. Nuclear explosions and dumping radioactive waste are banned. Scientists are free to investigate. Remember Level 1? Antarctica has no permanent residents, only researchers and support staff. This is the rulebook they work under.

cards.fact: Mining in Antarctica is banned.
cards.context: The Madrid Protocol of 1991 forbids all mineral resource activity except scientific research. It names Antarctica a natural reserve, devoted to peace and science. Whatever lies under the ice stays there.

learned: Seven countries claim Antarctica; three claims overlap

title: Checkpoint: Oceania and the Poles
objective: After this level you can describe Australia, the Pacific islands, the Arctic and Antarctica.
summary: The poles are opposites: the Arctic is ocean ringed by land, Antarctica land ringed by ocean. The high South Pole is far colder, and the poles take turns with six months of Sun.

cards.headline: The North and South Poles are exact opposites. And not just on the map.
cards.body: Level 10 showed why: switch 90° N to the other hemisphere and you get 90° S, straight through Earth's center. After this chapter, you can see how deep the opposites go.

cards.headline: Ocean up top, land down below
cards.body: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by continents. Antarctica is the reverse: a continent surrounded by ocean. So at the North Pole you'd stand on sea ice floating on the Arctic Ocean. At the South Pole you'd stand on the polar plateau, about 2,800 m above sea level. Same job title, completely different building.

cards.fact: In winter, the South Pole is far colder than the North Pole.
cards.context: Winter averages about −60 °C at the South Pole and about −40 °C at the North Pole. Two reasons, both from this chapter. Antarctica is high, and air gets colder with altitude. And the Arctic's ice floats on an ocean that's usually warmer than the air above it, while Antarctica gets little heat from the sea.

mascot.line: Six months of daylight, then six of dark. The poles invented the world's longest shift change.

cards.headline: Taking turns with the Sun
cards.body: Because Earth's axis is tilted, the two poles share the daylight by taking turns. For six months of the year the Sun never rises over one pole and never sets over the other. Then they swap. Level 4's tilt, pushed to its extreme: one pole's endless summer day is the other pole's endless winter night.

title: Eight Billion People
objective: After this level you can explain how the world population grew and where people live today.
summary: About 1 billion people lived on Earth around 1800; 8 billion by 2022, thanks to longer lives. Growth is slowing, and people cluster in Asia and north of the Equator.

cards.headline: Around 1800, the world held about 1 billion people. Now it holds 8.
cards.body: It took nearly all of human history to reach that first billion. The next seven arrived in about two centuries. So what changed, and where did everybody end up?

cards.headline: Soap, food and medicine
cards.body: For almost all of history, our numbers crept up slowly. Around 1800 they reached about 1 billion. Then the curve bent sharply upward, and on 15 November 2022 the UN marked the world passing 8 billion. The main reason is that people live longer: better public health, nutrition, hygiene and medicine. Humanity's great boom was powered less by magic than by soap, good food and a doctor down the road.

cards.fact: The boom is slowing down.
cards.context: Going from 7 to 8 billion took 12 years. The next billion should take about 15, arriving around 2037. The UN expects the total to peak at about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s. Think of a car that has taken its foot off the gas: still rolling forward, but coasting toward a stop.

cards.headline: Where everyone lives
cards.body: People are not spread like butter on toast. The Asia-Pacific region alone is home to about 60% of humanity. It holds the two giants, too: in April 2023, by UN estimates, India overtook China as the most populous country, after China's population had peaked in 2022 and begun to fall.

mascot.line: Nearly nine in ten of us on the top half of the globe. The Southern Hemisphere has plenty of elbow room.

cards.headline: A lopsided planet
cards.body: Remember Level 4's Equator, splitting Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres? The split is not fair. About 87% of people live in the Northern Hemisphere, which also holds about two-thirds of the land. If you're reading this, the odds say you're north of the Equator too.
