title: Cities
objective: After this level you can explain why cities grow and name the largest urban areas.
summary: Cities pull people in with jobs and opportunity, and boomed with industry. Megacities (10 million+) grew from 8 to 33; by the UN's 2025 count Jakarta, Dhaka and Tokyo are the largest.

cards.headline: Tokyo was long the world's biggest city. Then the UN measured again.
cards.body: In 2025 a UN report crowned Jakarta instead, using a new method. Nobody packed a single moving box that day. So how do cities grow, and how do you even measure one?

cards.headline: Why cities pull people in
cards.body: Cities work like magnets. People leave the countryside for jobs in factories and offices, and for better chances at school and a livelier life. Cities really began to boom in the 18th century, when large-scale industry arrived. Factories needed workers, and the workers came. That's how a market town becomes a skyline.

cards.fact: In 1975 the world had 8 megacities. By 2025 it had 33.
cards.context: A megacity is an urban area with 10 million people or more. Of today's 33, 19 are in Asia, which fits Level 91: the Asia-Pacific region is home to about 60% of humanity. Picture an entire country's worth of people sharing one subway map.

mascot.line: Same problem as Level 3's meridians: nobody can compare anything until everyone agrees where to measure from.

cards.headline: Where does a city end?
cards.body: Measuring a city sounds easy until you try to find its edge. Countries used to draw that line in different ways, so the UN's 2025 figures switched to one shared method. By that count, Jakarta leads with nearly 42 million people, Dhaka has almost 40 million and Tokyo 33 million. Dhaka is projected to take first place by 2050. City rankings, like milk, come with a date on them.

learned: Jobs and opportunity pull people into cities

title: Countries and Borders
objective: After this level you can explain how borders are drawn and why the count of countries varies.
summary: The UN has 193 members and 2 observer states; lists differ over places like Kosovo and Taiwan. Borders follow mountains and rivers, straight lines, or lines drawn by distant powers.

cards.headline: How many countries are there? 193? 195? It depends who you ask.
cards.body: Nobody here is bad at counting. Whether a place is a country depends partly on who agrees that it is one. Borders are the same: someone had to decide where to draw them.

cards.headline: The UN's list
cards.body: The most common answer comes from the United Nations: 193 member states. Add its two observer states, the Holy See and the State of Palestine, and you get 195. The newest member is South Sudan, independent since 2011. Places like Kosovo, which declared independence in 2008, and Taiwan are not UN members, so some lists count them and others don't. Every count is also a point of view.

cards.headline: Borders drawn by nature
cards.body: Some borders let the land do the talking. The border between France and Spain follows the crest of the Pyrenees mountains. For part of its length, the US-Mexico border follows a river, the Rio Grande. Mountains and rivers make borders you can see from a plane window, no painted line required.

cards.headline: Borders drawn with a ruler
cards.body: Other borders ignore the landscape entirely. Across much of the West, the Canada-US border simply follows the 49th parallel, a line of latitude you met in Level 3. Britain and the United States agreed on it in stages, in 1818 and 1846. It's a straight line on the map that no river would ever choose.

cards.headline: Lines that split people
cards.body: Borders drawn far away can cut straight through people's lives. In the 1800s and 1900s, European countries drew borders across Africa while ignoring the Indigenous communities already living there. Again and again, borders drawn without reference to the people on the ground have led to conflict and border disputes. A map line is thin; its consequences are not.

title: Languages of the World
objective: After this level you can name the world's most spoken languages and explain language families.
summary: Humans speak more than 7,000 languages, at least 40% endangered. English and Mandarin top a billion speakers each. English, Hindi and Persian share one ancestor: Proto-Indo-European.

cards.headline: Count to three in German, Latin or Sanskrit, and English echoes back.
cards.body: Drei. Tres. Trayas. Three languages spoken far apart in place and time, with a family resemblance you can hear. That echo is a clue to one of the biggest family trees on Earth.

cards.headline: A planet of 7,000 voices
cards.body: Humans speak more than 7,000 languages. That variety is shrinking, though: at least 40% of the world's languages are endangered. When a language falls silent, it takes a piece of cultural and intellectual heritage with it: songs, jokes and ways of describing the world that no dictionary fully captures.

cards.fact: Only two languages have more than a billion speakers.
cards.context: They're English and Mandarin Chinese. Count everyone who speaks a language and English comes out on top, because most of its speakers learned it as a second language. Count only native speakers and Mandarin wins. So which is the most spoken? It depends on whether you count the learners.

cards.headline: Languages have family trees
cards.body: Languages have parents too. A language family is a group descended from one ancestor. English, Spanish, Russian, Hindi and Persian are all Indo-European cousins, spoken across most of Europe and much of South and Southwest Asia. Their shared parent, Proto-Indo-European, was probably spoken around 4000 BCE. Nobody has a recording; scholars reconstructed it.

mascot.line: Linguists: detectives whose best clue is how you say three.

cards.headline: How we know
cards.body: How do you prove a family with no birth certificate? In the 19th century, scholars systematically compared languages' sounds, grammar and vocabulary. Words like three, drei, tres, treis and trayas line up too neatly to be chance. They all come from one Proto-Indo-European root. Same ancestor, different accents, after thousands of years of drifting apart.

title: Religions Around the World
objective: After this level you can describe the world's major religions and where they are practiced.
summary: Christians are about 29% of the world, Muslims 26%, the unaffiliated 24%. Most Muslims, Hindus and Buddhists live in Asia-Pacific; sub-Saharan Africa now has the most Christians.

cards.headline: The world's largest religion now has more followers in Africa than in Europe.
cards.body: If you picture Christianity centered on Europe, your map needs an update. Religion has a geography, and that geography moves.

cards.headline: The big picture
cards.body: No single religion claims a majority of humanity. Christians are the largest group: about 2.3 billion people, or about 29% of the world in 2020. Muslims follow at about 26%. Third place is a surprise: people with no religion at all, about 24%. Hindus make up about 15% and Buddhists about 4%. Roughly one in four people on Earth checks the 'none' box.

mascot.line: Picture a 'typical' Muslim and you might picture the Middle East. The numbers point further east.

cards.headline: Faith follows people
cards.body: Level 91 put about 60% of humanity in the Asia-Pacific region. Religion tracks that crowd. About 59% of Muslims live in Asia-Pacific, so most Muslims live east of the Middle East, not in it. For Hindus the share is 99%, and for Buddhists 98%. Two of the world's big religions are almost entirely Asian.

cards.headline: On the move
cards.body: Religious maps change. By 2020, sub-Saharan Africa had overtaken Europe as the region with the most Christians, home to about 31% of them. Meanwhile, from 2010 to 2020, Muslims were the fastest-growing major group, and people with no religion also grew as a share of the world. A religious map, like a city ranking, needs a date on it.

title: Feeding the World
objective: After this level you can explain where the world's food is grown and which crops feed the most people.
summary: Rice, maize and wheat give about 60% of the world's food energy. Rice, mostly grown in Asia-Pacific, feeds almost half of humanity. Almost half of habitable land is farmed.

cards.headline: Look at your plate. It probably started as rice, corn or wheat.
cards.body: Those three crops supply about 60% of the food energy people eat. The menu of humanity is surprisingly short, and it takes a startling amount of land.

cards.headline: A very short menu
cards.body: Just 15 crop plants provide 90% of the world's food energy. Three of them, rice, maize (corn) and wheat, supply two-thirds of that on their own: about 60% of all the energy humans eat. Bread, tortillas, noodles, porridge: the world's breakfast table is mostly variations on three plants.

cards.headline: The rice bowl
cards.body: Rice alone feeds almost half of humanity. More than 90% of the world's rice is grown and eaten in the Asia-Pacific region. Put that next to Level 91, where about 60% of people live in that same region, and it clicks: the rice fields sit right where the people are.

mascot.line: Half the livable land on Earth, mostly for cows, sheep and their dinners. That is a lot of pasture.

cards.fact: Almost half of the world's habitable land is farmed.
cards.context: And more than three-quarters of that farmland goes to livestock, for grazing and for growing animal feed. Yet meat, dairy and farmed fish supply less than a fifth of the world's calories. Most farmland, in other words, feeds animals first and people second.

title: Resources and Wealth
objective: After this level you can explain how resources like oil, metals and water shape where wealth is found.
summary: Venezuela has the most proven oil; Congo mines most cobalt. Yet resource wealth often means slower growth, unless reinvested, as in Botswana. Fresh water is scarce everywhere.

cards.headline: The country with the most proven oil in the ground is not Saudi Arabia.
cards.body: It's Venezuela. And owning buried treasure, it turns out, is a very different thing from getting rich off it.

cards.headline: Treasure is unevenly spread
cards.body: Nature did not share out its resources fairly. Venezuela holds the world's largest proven crude oil reserves, ahead of Saudi Arabia. The Democratic Republic of the Congo mines about three-quarters of the world's cobalt. Rocks formed where they formed, long before anyone drew the borders of Level 93 around them.

cards.headline: The resource curse
cards.body: You'd expect a country sitting on oil or minerals to be rich. Often it isn't. Economists call this the resource curse: countries with abundant natural resources often grow more slowly than countries with fewer. One reason is conflict: when a treasure is worth fighting over, people fight over it.

mascot.line: Turning diamonds into schools. That is what I call a sparkling investment.

cards.headline: Botswana's way out
cards.body: The curse is a pattern, not a law. Botswana relies heavily on diamond exports, yet it's widely seen as having dodged it. The trick: money from minerals is reinvested, in infrastructure, health and education. A mine empties eventually. A well-built road and an educated workforce keep paying out.

cards.fact: Earth is covered in water, but very little of it is drinkable.
cards.context: Remember Level 1: about 71% of Earth's surface is water. Yet the oceans hold about 96.5% of all Earth's water, and it's salty. Of the fresh water, over 68% is locked in ice and glaciers. The one resource every person needs is the one the planet keeps mostly salted or frozen.

title: People on the Move
objective: After this level you can explain why people migrate and where the biggest movements happen.
summary: Push and pull factors move people. About 304 million were international migrants in 2024; the US hosts the most. Most of the 123.2 million forcibly displaced stayed in their own countries.

cards.headline: About 1 in 27 people lives in a country they moved to.
cards.body: That's a lot of suitcases: about 304 million people. It also means most people never move countries at all. So why do people go, and where?

cards.headline: Push and pull
cards.body: Every move has two sides. Push factors drive people away: war, food shortages, floods. Pull factors draw them somewhere: jobs, a nicer climate, a better food supply. The move can be internal, within one country, or international, to a different country. Remember Level 92's city jobs luring people from the countryside? That was a pull factor all along.

cards.fact: About 304 million people are international migrants.
cards.context: That's about 3.7% of humanity as of 2024, roughly 1 in 27 people. The United States hosts more of them than any other country. It's a huge number and a small share at the same time: nearly everyone else still lives in the country they call home.

cards.headline: When the push is violent
cards.body: At the end of 2024, 123.2 million people had been forced from home by persecution, conflict, violence or human rights violations. Most never crossed a border: 83.4 million were displaced inside their own countries. Refugees, the ones who flee to a new country, mostly stay close too: 67% are hosted by neighbouring countries. Most people running from danger run as short a distance as they can.

title: Humans Change the Planet
objective: After this level you can explain how farming, cities and pollution reshape the land and the sea.
summary: Diverting rivers for cotton shrank the Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake. Farm and city runoff creates a dead zone off the Mississippi every summer.

cards.headline: People made one of the world's biggest lakes mostly disappear.
cards.body: The Aral Sea was once the fourth-largest lake on Earth. No drought emptied it. In the 1960s its rivers were redirected to grow crops, and the lake paid the price.

cards.headline: Rivers into cotton
cards.body: In the 1960s, the Soviet Union diverted the region's two major rivers to irrigate the desert for cotton and other crops. The desert bloomed. The lake, starved of its inflow, began to shrink. In 2014, the eastern lobe of the South Aral Sea disappeared completely. Where fishing boats once floated, there is now dry, dusty ground.

mascot.line: A lake turned into a desert to water a desert. Geography has a dark sense of humor.

cards.headline: The bill arrives
cards.body: A big lake softens the weather around it. Without it, local winters grew colder and summers hotter and drier. Wind picked up dust from the exposed lakebed, carrying farm chemicals that harmed crops and people's health. The fisheries collapsed. There is a hopeful footnote: a dam finished in 2005 helped the North Aral Sea's fisheries rebound.

cards.headline: Dead zones at sea
cards.body: The sea can be changed from far upstream, too. Every summer, excess nutrients from farms and cities across the Mississippi River basin wash into the Gulf and feed huge blooms of algae. When the algae die and decompose, they use up the water's oxygen. The result is a dead zone: water with so little oxygen it can kill fish and other marine life.
